lessons.title: Scarcity, choice, scale of preference and opportunity cost

steps.title: One note at the provision shop
steps.display: ₦1,000 in pocket  vs  bread + egg + recharge card + pure water
working: Wants exceed cash, so you rank them and pick the top items.
The best item you leave on the shelf is your opportunity cost.
steps.narration: Picture yourself at a Lagos provision stall with one thousand naira. You cannot buy everything on your list. Whatever top item you leave behind is the real cost.

steps.title: Wants, scarcity, choice and scale of preference
steps.display: Unlimited wants + Scarce means (alternative uses) → Scale of preference → Choice
working: Robbins (1932): Economics studies human behaviour between ends and scarce means with alternative uses.
Wants: desires for goods and services; basic needs (food, shelter, clothing) plus endless new desires.
Scarcity: resources are limited relative to demand (not merely rare).
Scale of preference: ranking wants from most pressing to least pressing; following it shows rationality.
steps.narration: Why do we study economics at all? Because human desires never end, while money, time and land run out. Suppose you have twenty naira for school items. Ranking your exercise book above shoes lets you pick wisely. Putting needs in order before choosing is rational behaviour.

steps.title: Opportunity cost versus money cost
steps.display: Opportunity cost (real or true cost) = Next best alternative foregone  ≠  Money cost
working: Money cost: actual cash paid for an item (accountant's view).
Opportunity cost (real or true cost): value of the single next best alternative sacrificed (economist's view).
Example (Anyaele p. 115): With ₦10, buying a textbook instead of a shirt gives money cost = ₦10, real cost = the shirt.
steps.narration: Accountants look at the receipt. Economists look at what you gave up. That sacrificed option is the real cost, even when no cash changes hands. Say a farmer uses her only plot for cassava instead of yam. Her opportunity cost is the yam harvest she forfeited.

steps.title: Basic economic problems and efficient resource use
steps.display: What to produce  |  How to produce  |  For whom to produce  |  Efficiency
working: What to produce: which goods and services, and in what quantities (e.g. food vs defence).
How to produce: choosing least-cost techniques — labour-intensive (more labour) vs capital-intensive (more machines).
For whom to produce: who receives output (income in capitalism; needs and contributions in socialism).
Efficiency (Pareto optimality): impossible to produce more of one good without reducing another.
steps.narration: Scarcity forces every society, rich or poor, to answer three core questions. What goods should we make? Which method uses the least cost? Who gets the finished products? For example, a Nigerian textile mill can hire more workers or buy looms. Using resources fully without waste achieves efficiency.

steps.title: The Production Possibility Frontier (PPF / PPC)
steps.display: On PPF = efficient  |  Inside = waste or unemployment  |  Outside = unattainable (scarcity)
working: PPF (or PPC / PPB): maximum combinations of two goods producible with fixed resources and technology.
Downward slope illustrates choice and opportunity cost (more of X means less of Y).
Concave (bowed-out) shape reflects increasing opportunity cost from diminishing returns.
Points inside (e.g. unemployed labour) can expand output without sacrificing either good.
steps.narration: Think of a boundary line around what an economy can actually make. Points right on that curve show zero waste. Points inside mean idle workers or machines. Points outside are impossible right now because resources are scarce. Take a country making guns and butter. More guns means less butter.

steps.title: PPF shifts and economic growth
steps.display: Outward shift of PPF = economic growth (more resources, better technology, or higher skills)
working: Balanced outward shift: economy can produce more of both goods (e.g. better fertiliser for all crops).
Biased outward shift: technology improves one good only, pivoting the PPF out on that axis.
Inward shift: war, natural disaster, or resource depletion shrinks productive capacity.
steps.narration: Can an economy ever reach points outside today's boundary? Yes, when the whole curve shifts outward. That happens when a nation gains new tools, more capital, or trained workers. Imagine better fertiliser boosting yields of both yam and cocoa. Suddenly the economy enjoys real growth.

steps.title: Read the Nigerian crop PPF table (Anyaele Table 4.2)
steps.display: A: (3,500 food, 0 cash)  →  B: (2,800 food, 600 cash)  →  C: (2,000 food, 1,000 cash)
working: All output figures are in tonnes per month.
Move A → B: cash crops increase from 0 to 600 (+600 tonnes).
Food crops fall from 3,500 to 2,800 (−700 tonnes).
Opportunity cost of the first 600 tonnes of cash crops = 700 tonnes of food crops.
steps.narration: Let us trace a real table from Anyaele. At the top combination, Nigeria puts every farm input into food crops. To get six hundred tonnes of cash crops, food drops from three thousand five hundred to two thousand eight hundred. That seven hundred tonne drop is the sacrifice.

steps.title: Calculate opportunity cost per tonne from B to C
steps.display: Opportunity cost per tonne of cash crops = \frac{Δ Food}{Δ Cash} = \frac{800}{400} = 2 tonnes of food
working: From B to C: ΔFood = 2,800 − 2,000 = 800 tonnes sacrificed.
ΔCash = 1,000 − 600 = 400 tonnes gained.
Cost per tonne of cash crops = \frac{800}{400} = 2 tonnes of food crops.
steps.narration: Wait, let us find the cost for each single tonne as we keep shifting land. Between the second and third rows, food drops by eight hundred while cash rises by four hundred. Divide eight hundred by four hundred. Each extra tonne of cash crop now costs two tonnes of food.

steps.title: Classify points inside and outside the PPF
steps.display: Point X: (1,300 food, 1,000 cash)  vs  Point Z: (2,800 food, 1,500 cash)
working: At 1,000 cash crops, the frontier (C) allows 2,000 food crops.
Point X produces only 1,300 food < 2,000 → inside PPF (unemployment or waste).
At 1,500 cash crops, the frontier (D) allows 1,300 food crops.
Point Z demands 2,800 food > 1,300 → outside PPF (unattainable without growth).
steps.narration: Now compare two test points against the table. At one thousand tonnes of cash crops, efficient farms produce two thousand tonnes of food. Producing just one thousand three hundred leaves resources idle inside the curve. Asking for two thousand eight hundred alongside fifteen hundred cash crops lies beyond reach.

steps.title: JAMB-style practice question
steps.display: (Practice) Tunde has ₦4,000 and ranks his wants: (1) Maths textbook ₦4,000, (2) School sandals ₦4,000, (3) Shirt ₦3,500, (4) Watch ₦2,500. If he acts rationally and buys the textbook, what is its opportunity cost?
working: A. ₦4,000  |  B. The school sandals  |  C. The sandals, shirt and watch combined  |  D. Zero
steps.narration: Try this practice question carefully. Notice Tunde already ranked his items by importance before spending. He has just four thousand naira, and each top item takes the whole sum. We want the economic opportunity cost of buying the book, not the price tag.

steps.title: Identify what Tunde chose and what ranked next
steps.display: Budget = ₦4,000  →  Chooses rank (1) Maths textbook  |  Next best = rank (2) School sandals
working: Rationality means picking the highest-ranked affordable item first: Maths textbook (₦4,000).
With ₦4,000 spent, he can no longer afford rank (2) School sandals.
Rank (2) is the single highest alternative he gave up.
steps.narration: First check how a rational buyer behaves. He picks the top item on his list, which is the textbook. Once that money leaves his pocket, his next most wanted item slips away. Which item sat right in second place? The sandals. Keep that second spot locked in.

steps.title: Rule out the distractors and confirm the answer
steps.display: Answer: The school sandals (rank 2)
working: ₦4,000 is the money cost, not the opportunity cost (rules out the cash figure).
Summing sandals + shirt + watch assumes he could buy all three with ₦4,000 (false).
Zero cost is false because scarce cash meant sacrificing rank (2).
Correct choice: The school sandals.
steps.narration: Let us knock out the traps one by one. Four thousand naira is only the money cost, not the real sacrifice. He could never buy sandals, shirt and watch together with four thousand naira, so summing them fails. Zero cost ignores scarcity. Therefore the sandals are the true cost.

steps.title: Confusing opportunity cost with money cost
steps.display: Wrong: Opportunity cost = ₦500 paid  |  Right: Money cost = ₦500; Opportunity cost = best item foregone
working: Cash spent is money cost (explicit payment).
Even a free-to-attend class has an opportunity cost (lost sleep or wage).
Always pick the sacrificed alternative, not the naira amount.
steps.narration: Here is a classic exam trap. Many candidates see a price in naira and pick that number for opportunity cost. Remember, cash paid is money cost. Real cost is the alternative you gave up. Even reading for free carries a time sacrifice.

steps.title: Summing all unchosen items instead of the next best
steps.display: Wrong: Cost = item 2 + item 3 + item 4  |  Right: Cost = single next best alternative (item 2)
working: Limited funds allowed only one of the competing items anyway.
Therefore, you only sacrificed the single best alternative next in line.
steps.narration: Do not add up every single thing you did not buy. With limited money, you could never have owned all those unchosen items at once. You only lost the one best alternative right behind your choice. Pick that second ranked item alone.

steps.title: Mixing up movement inside the PPF with economic growth
steps.display: Wrong: Moving from inside PPF to the curve = growth  |  Right: That reduces waste; growth shifts PPF outward
working: Inside → On PPF: puts idle or unemployed resources to work (same capacity).
Outward shift of PPF: expands productive capacity itself (economic growth).
steps.narration: Watch this diagram distinction closely. Moving from inside the curve onto the curve gives more output, yes. Yet capacity did not grow. Society simply put idle workers back to work. True economic growth pushes the entire boundary line outward through better technology or more resources.

steps.title: From unlimited wants to rational choices on the frontier
steps.display: Scarcity → Scale of preference → Choice → Opportunity cost (PPF slope)
working: Scarcity forces what, how, and for whom decisions.
Real cost is the next best alternative foregone; PPF maps trade-offs, waste, and growth.
steps.narration: Everything in this chapter flows from one chain. Wants have no limit, but resources do. That forces us to rank needs, make choices, and accept opportunity cost. On a frontier graph, choices trace the curve, waste sits inside, and real growth shifts the whole curve outward.

quickCheck.stem: (Practice) If an economy moves from a point inside its production possibility curve (PPC) to a point on the curve, this shows that

options.text: new technology has shifted the economy's productive capacity outward
options.why: New technology shifts the entire PPC outward, whereas moving from inside to the curve uses existing capacity.

options.text: previously idle or wasted resources are now being efficiently employed
options.why: Points inside the PPC show unemployment or waste of resources, so moving onto the curve means full, efficient use of existing resources.

options.text: the economy has reached a previously unattainable combination outside its resources
options.why: Unattainable combinations lie outside the PPC, not on the existing curve.

options.text: opportunity cost has been completely eliminated in the economy
options.why: Scarcity remains, so moving along the PPC still involves opportunity cost; only moving from inside can raise one good without cutting the other.

steps.title: Who runs the shops and who runs the power grid
steps.display: Private provision shop (profit)  +  Public road & power network (welfare)
working: Every society chooses who owns resources and who decides what gets made.
Some leave it to market prices, some to the state, and most blend both.
steps.narration: Walk down any Nigerian street. Private shops sell bread for profit, while government builds public roads. How a country shares those duties defines its economic system.

steps.title: Free enterprise or capitalist economic system
steps.display: Private ownership  +  Price mechanism  +  Profit motive  +  Minimum state role
working: Ownership: private individuals own and control all or most means of production and distribution.
Coordination: resources allocated via market price signals; profit motive guides production.
Features: freedom of enterprise and choice, competition, specialisation, labour as a marketable commodity.
Merits: self-regulating, innovation, hard work, quality, consumer choice. Demerits: inequality, private monopoly, exploitation, job insecurity.
steps.narration: In a free market system, private owners run farms, factories and shops with minimal state control. Prices act like traffic lights, showing producers where profit lies. Take a private bakery in Ibadan raising bread output when demand lifts prices. Rivalry brings innovation, though wide income gaps can follow.

steps.title: Centrally planned or socialist economic system
steps.display: State ownership  +  Central planning  +  Social welfare motive
working: Ownership: state collectively owns and controls all or major means of production and distribution (Karl Marx, 1818–1883).
Coordination: central planning board replaces market price signals; non-market economy.
Motive: goods produced to satisfy citizens' needs, not private profit; labour is not a marketable commodity.
Merits: equitable distribution, no private monopoly, job security. Demerits: bureaucracy, low initiative, little choice, lower quality.
steps.narration: Now flip the switch completely. Under socialism, the government owns factories and land on behalf of all citizens. State planners decide output targets instead of market prices. Imagine a central ministry setting how many loaves every town gets. Everyone gets basic security, yet bureaucracy often slows quality and innovation.

steps.title: Mixed economic system
steps.display: Private sector (private goods, profit)  +  Public sector (public goods, regulation)
working: Both private and public ownership of means of production exist side by side.
Government regulates, supervises and holds exclusive control over selected strategic areas.
Nigeria and most developing countries practise a mixed economy (pure capitalism or socialism rarely exists).
Merits: blends enterprise with welfare protection. Demerits: goal conflict, corruption, inequality and inefficiency.
steps.narration: Real countries rarely stick to one pure extreme. A mixed economy lets private businesses chase profit while the state provides public services and enforces rules. Nigeria works this way. For instance, private traders sell food while the state builds highways and regulates banks. Balancing both sides remains tricky.

steps.title: Solving the basic economic problems in each system
steps.display: What, How, and For Whom  →  Prices & income (Capitalism)  vs  State & needs (Socialism)
working: What to produce: Capitalism follows high prices and profit; Socialism follows state assessment of citizens' needs.
How to produce: Capitalism uses private least-cost methods; Socialism uses state and public resources.
For whom to produce: Capitalism distributes by income and ability to pay; Socialism distributes by needs and contributions.
Mixed economy: both private markets and public authorities share all three decisions.
steps.narration: Every society faces what, how and for whom to produce, yet each system answers differently. Suppose a country needs shoes and clinics. A capitalist market builds whatever buyers with cash pay for. A socialist board allocates both by citizens' needs. A mixed economy uses markets plus public budgets.

steps.title: Reforming the mix: nationalisation, commercialisation, privatisation
steps.display: Nationalisation (private → state)  |  Commercialisation (state + profit)  |  Privatisation (state → private)
working: Nationalisation: transfer from private to state ownership (with compensation) to curb exploitation or control key sectors.
Commercialisation: running state-owned enterprises primarily to make profit while keeping state ownership.
Privatisation: transferring ownership, control or management of public enterprises to the private sector to curb waste.
JAMB contemporary reforms also include deregulation, banking sector consolidation and cash policy reform.
steps.narration: Mixed economies shift the boundary between state and market through reforms. When a state firm becomes a loss-making white elephant, government may step in. For example, Nigeria can commercialise a public corporation so it chases profit, or privatise it to private owners. Deregulation similarly opens sectors to competition.

steps.title: Compare 'What to produce' for housing across systems
steps.display: Scenario: Should resources build luxury estates or low-cost public housing?
working: Capitalism: private developers build luxury estates if high prices yield bigger profits.
Socialism: central planners order low-cost housing to meet citizens' basic shelter needs.
Mixed economy: private firms build commercial estates while government funds social housing.
steps.narration: Let us compare how the three systems handle a real choice like housing. Where private profit rules, builders chase whichever homes fetch the highest price. Under central planning, officials prioritise basic shelter for all citizens. A mixed economy lets private developers build while government supports public housing.

steps.title: Compare 'How to produce' across systems
steps.display: Choice of technique: labour-intensive vs capital-intensive
working: Capitalism: private firms compare factor prices and pick the least-cost method to maximise profit.
Socialism: the state deploys public capital and workers according to the national plan (aiming at full employment).
Mixed economy: private builders minimise costs; public works may deliberately favour labour-intensive jobs.
steps.narration: Next, look at the building method itself. Private capitalist firms compare wage rates against machine rentals, picking whichever costs less per house. Socialist planners assign state equipment and public workers to keep everyone employed. In a mixed system, private builders cut costs while public projects create jobs.

steps.title: Compare 'For whom to produce' across systems
steps.display: Capitalism → ability to pay (income)  |  Socialism → needs & contributions  |  Mixed → both
working: Capitalism: households with higher incomes buy better homes; low earners get less.
Socialism: housing is allocated by family need and work contribution, curbing rich–poor gaps.
Mixed economy: market prices allocate private homes, while state subsidies aid lower-income citizens.
steps.narration: Finally, who actually moves into the finished houses? Under capitalism, your wallet decides, so higher earners secure better homes. Under socialism, distribution follows household needs and contributions to society. A mixed economy pairs private sales with subsidised public schemes so lower earners are not left behind.

steps.title: JAMB-style practice question
steps.display: (Practice) In a free enterprise economy, the problem of 'for whom to produce' is primarily solved by
working: A. directives of a central planning board
B. consumers' income and purchasing power in the market
C. equal sharing regardless of individual output
D. government rationing committees
steps.narration: Here is a practice question on economic systems. Pay close attention to the wording. It asks specifically about a free enterprise economy and the third basic problem, who receives the goods. Do not rush. Let us test each choice against how capitalism actually distributes output.

steps.title: Recall how capitalism allocates output
steps.display: Free enterprise = Capitalism  →  Price mechanism + Private income
working: In capitalism, goods are produced for sale in the market.
Anyaele p. 40 (§3.3): 'one's income determines the type and quantity of goods and services he enjoys in a capitalist system.'
steps.narration: Remember, free enterprise is another name for capitalism. In a market system, shops do not give away goods by committee or equal shares. Producers sell to buyers who can pay the market price. Therefore, a household's income and purchasing power decide what it takes home.

steps.title: Eliminate the socialist distractors
steps.display: Answer: Consumers' income and purchasing power in the market
working: Central planning board directives belong to socialism, not free enterprise.
Equal sharing regardless of output does not describe market distribution.
Government rationing committees reflect state control, not free enterprise.
Correct choice: consumers' income and purchasing power in the market.
steps.narration: Now rule out the other three choices cleanly. Central planning boards belong to a controlled socialist economy, not free enterprise. Equal sharing without regard to price ignores market exchange. Government rationing is also state control. That leaves consumers' income and purchasing power as our clear winner.

steps.title: Assuming real countries operate pure capitalism or pure socialism
steps.display: Wrong: USA = 100% pure capitalism  |  Right: Pure capitalism and pure socialism rarely exist; Nigeria is mixed
working: Anyaele p. 111 & p. 113: pure market capitalism and pure socialism do not really exist in practice.
Even market-led economies have public schools, defence, and regulation; Nigeria operates a mixed economy.
steps.narration: Do not treat textbook models as pure snapshots of real countries. Even market-heavy nations collect taxes, run courts and regulate banks. Likewise, planned economies still allow some private trade. Anyaele reminds us that pure forms hardly exist, and Nigeria itself runs a mixed economic system.

steps.title: Confusing commercialisation with privatisation
steps.display: Wrong: Commercialisation sells the firm  |  Right: Commercialisation keeps state ownership (profit aim); Privatisation transfers to private sector
working: Commercialisation: enterprise remains state-owned, but must operate for profit.
Privatisation: ownership, control or management shifts from public to private hands.
Nationalisation: moves in the opposite direction, from private to state ownership.
steps.narration: Exam questions love testing these two reform words side by side. Commercialisation does not sell a government corporation to private buyers. It simply orders the state firm to stop losing money and chase profit. Privatisation goes further by handing ownership, control or management over to private investors.

steps.title: Mixing up 'for whom to produce' in capitalism and socialism
steps.display: Wrong: Capitalism distributes by need  |  Right: Capitalism → income; Socialism → needs and contributions
working: Capitalism: income and purchasing power determine goods enjoyed.
Socialism: goods distributed according to citizens' needs and contributions.
steps.narration: Keep the distribution rule straight between the two rival systems. Under capitalism, need alone does not put food on your table. Only income backed by purchasing power unlocks goods in the market. Under socialism, the state distributes output according to citizens' needs and their contributions.

steps.title: Ownership, coordination and motive separate the systems
steps.display: Capitalism (private + price + profit)  |  Socialism (state + plan + welfare)  |  Mixed (both, as in Nigeria)
working: Compare systems by who owns resources, how decisions are coordinated, and what motive drives output.
Reforms like nationalisation, commercialisation and privatisation adjust the public–private balance.
steps.narration: To master economic systems, always ask three quick questions. Who owns the farms and factories? Do prices or state planners coordinate output? Does profit or social welfare drive decisions? Once you know those answers, comparing capitalism, socialism and Nigeria's mixed economy becomes straightforward.

quickCheck.stem: (Practice) When a government retains ownership of a public enterprise but directs it to operate primarily to make profit, the policy is called

options.why: Nationalisation is the takeover of a private enterprise into state ownership, not making an existing state firm profit-driven.
Privatisation transfers ownership, control or management of a public enterprise to the private sector.
Commercialisation keeps the enterprise under state ownership while requiring it to run with the primary aim of making profit.
Collectivisation pools private farms or assets into collective state control, rather than running a state enterprise for profit.

lessons.title: Demand, its determinants and elasticity of demand

steps.title: Wanting garri versus buying garri
steps.display: Effective demand = Willingness to buy + Ability to pay (at a price and time)
working: Dreaming of a plate of rice = mere want.
Standing at the stall with ₦500 ready to pay = effective demand.
steps.narration: Every passerby might crave cold pure water under the hot sun. Only the buyer holding naira and ready to hand it over creates real demand.

steps.title: Effective demand, law of demand and ceteris paribus
steps.display: Normal law of demand: P ↑ ⇒ Q_{d} ↓  and  P ↓ ⇒ Q_{d} ↑ (ceteris paribus)
working: Effective demand needs willingness, ability to pay, a set price and time.
Ceteris paribus means all other factors remain unchanged.
Normal demand curve slopes downward from left to right.
steps.narration: Economists separate wishing from buying. You need desire, cash, a set price, and a time period. Hold everything else steady, and higher prices push buyers back. Say garri jumps from three hundred to five hundred naira a paint bucket. Most shoppers immediately buy fewer buckets.

steps.title: Change in quantity demanded versus change in demand
steps.display: Own price changes Q_{d} (along curve)  |  Non-price factors shift D
working: Movement along curve: expansion (P ↓, Q_{d} ↑) or contraction (P ↑, Q_{d} ↓).
Shift right (D_{0} → D_{1}): higher income, taste, population or festive season.
Shift left (D_{0} → D_{2}): higher tax, lower income or cheaper substitutes.
steps.narration: Watch this distinction closely. When only the good's own price changes, buyers slide up or down the same line. When something outside price changes, the whole line jumps. Suppose salaries double across your town. People buy more yam at every single price, shifting the entire line outward.

steps.title: Four types of demand and abnormal demand
steps.display: Types: Derived, Joint, Competitive, Composite  |  Abnormal: P ↑ ⇒ Q_{d} ↑
working: Derived: labour wanted to produce goods. Joint: car and petrol together.
Competitive: close substitutes (Omo vs Elephant). Composite: palm oil for food, soap, pomade.
Abnormal upward curve: Giffen staples, ostentation, expected price rises, rare goods.
steps.narration: Goods connect in four ways. You buy petrol because you drive a car, which shows joint demand. Bakers hire workers only because people want bread, showing derived demand. Sometimes higher prices even boost buying, like gold watches worn to show wealth or staples like garri during hardship.

steps.title: Price elasticity of demand and its five types
steps.display: PED = \frac{%ΔQ_{d}}{%ΔP}  |  E > 1 (elastic), E < 1 (inelastic), E = 1 (unitary)
working: Extreme cases: E = 0 (perfectly inelastic, vertical) and E = ∞ (perfectly elastic, horizontal).
Key determinants: close substitutes, necessity (salt), habit, income level and multiple uses.
steps.narration: Elasticity asks how strongly buyers react when price moves. Suppose a twenty percent price jump cuts buying by only ten percent. Dividing gives zero point five, so buyers barely budge. Salt has almost no close substitutes. Families keep buying it even when its price climbs.

steps.title: Income elasticity, cross elasticity and importance
steps.display: YED = \frac{%ΔQ_{d}}{%ΔI}  |  CED = \frac{%ΔQ_{x}}{%ΔP_{y}}
working: YED > 0: normal good (rice, +1.6). YED < 0: inferior or Giffen good.
CED > 0: substitutes (Omo and Elephant). CED < 0: complements (car and petrol).
Importance: guides seller pricing, tax revenue choices and consumer spending plans.
steps.narration: We can also check how income or a rival's price affects buyers. When a pay raise makes a family buy more rice, income elasticity stays positive. Governments check this before setting taxes. Taxing necessities brings steady revenue without killing sales.

steps.title: Read the price schedule and find percentage change in quantity
steps.display: Agege bread rises from ₦50 to ₦70; Q_{d} falls from 200 to 160 loaves. Find |PED|.
steps.narration: Let us solve a bakery pricing problem together. First, pull out the starting price and starting quantity, because every percentage starts from the old values. Bread buying dropped by forty loaves out of two hundred. That means quantity fell by twenty percent.

steps.title: Calculate the percentage change in price
steps.narration: Now do the exact same thing for price. Remember why we convert both to percentages. We cannot fairly compare naira against loaves of bread. Bread went up by twenty naira from fifty naira. Dividing twenty by fifty gives a forty percent jump.

steps.title: Divide percentage changes and classify the demand
steps.display: |PED| = \left|\frac{−20%}{+40%}\right| = 0.50  ⇒  Inelastic demand (0 < 0.50 < 1)
working: Since 0.50 < 1, demand for Agege bread is fairly inelastic.
Revenue check: ₦50 × 200 = ₦10,000 → ₦70 × 160 = ₦11,200 (revenue rises).
steps.narration: Put the quantity percentage on top and the price percentage underneath. Twenty divided by forty gives zero point five zero. Notice that price jumped twice as much as buying dropped. Because zero point five zero is below one, demand is inelastic, so total revenue actually rose.

steps.title: JAMB-style practice question
steps.display: (Practice) When Omo price rises from ₦200 to ₦250, demand for Elephant detergent rises from 300 to 360 packets. Find CED and the relationship. (a) −0.80, complements (b) +0.80, substitutes (c) +1.25, substitutes (d) −1.25, complements
working: Target: Cross elasticity of demand (CED) between two detergents.
P_{Omo}: ₦200 → ₦250  |  Q_{Elephant}: 300 → 360 packets
steps.narration: Here is a practice question on cross elasticity. Two detergent prices and quantities appear together, so keep each product in its proper place. Before calculating, look at what happened when Omo got dearer. More shoppers grabbed Elephant instead. That single clue already tells you their relationship.

steps.title: Compute both percentage changes from initial values
working: Elephant quantity rose by 60 packets from 300 ⇒ +20%.
Omo price rose by ₦50 from ₦200 ⇒ +25%.
steps.narration: Find each percentage change starting from the original numbers. Elephant sales grew by sixty packets out of three hundred, giving plus twenty percent. Meanwhile, Omo increased by fifty naira from two hundred, giving plus twenty five percent. Keep both plus signs because direction matters here.

steps.title: Compute CED and eliminate wrong choices
steps.display: CED = \frac{+20%}{+25%} = +0.80  ⇒  Substitutes (competitive demand)
working: CED = +0.80 > 0, so the two goods are close substitutes.
Rule out −0.80 and −1.25 (complements give negative CED).
Rule out +1.25 (that flips %ΔP over %ΔQ). Correct answer: +0.80, substitutes.
steps.narration: Divide twenty percent by twenty five percent to get positive zero point eight zero. Because both moved upward together, they cannot be complements, which carry negative signs. Also avoid one point two five, which flips price onto the top. That leaves positive zero point eight zero, substitutes.

steps.title: Movement along the curve versus shift of the curve
steps.display: Wrong: own price shifts the demand curve  |  Right: own price moves Q_{d} along the same curve
working: Own price change → movement along D (change in quantity demanded).
Income, tastes, population or related prices → shift of D (change in demand).
steps.narration: Students constantly swap these two phrases under exam pressure. Remember why price stays on the vertical axis. Whenever the good's own price changes, you stay on the same curve and slide. Only outside factors like salary or fashion pick up the whole curve and move it.

steps.title: Using the wrong base or flipping price over quantity
steps.display: Wrong: \frac{500}{1500} ÷ \frac{5}{5} = 0.33 or \frac{%ΔP}{%ΔQ}  |  Right: \frac{ΔQ}{Q_{1}} ÷ \frac{ΔP}{P_{1}}
working: Correct using initial point: |PED| = \frac{50%}{50%} = 1.00.
Trap: dividing by new values (1,500 and 5) wrongly gives 0.33.
steps.narration: Two arithmetic traps wreck easy elasticity marks. First, always measure percentage change from the starting price and quantity, never the final values. Second, put quantity on top and price underneath. Putting price on top flips a zero point five answer straight into two.

steps.title: Composite versus joint demand and negative income elasticity
steps.display: Composite = 1 good, many uses  |  Joint = 2+ goods, 1 want  |  YED < 0 = inferior good
working: Palm oil for cooking, soap and pomade = composite demand (one good, many uses).
Car and petrol = joint or complementary demand (several goods, one want).
YED < 0 means higher income lowers demand (inferior or Giffen goods).
steps.narration: Do not mix up composite demand with complementary demand. Complementary goods work as a team, like a pen and an exercise book. Composite means one single item serves many jobs, like palm oil. Also remember that negative income elasticity marks an inferior good, not a normal one.

steps.title: Own price slides along the curve; elasticity measures responsiveness
steps.display: Effective demand (willing + able)  |  Own P → Q_{d} moves  |  Other factors → D shifts  |  E = \frac{%ΔQ}{%Δother}
working: Always compute percentage changes from the initial values and keep %ΔQ on top.
steps.narration: Keep three big anchors in mind for demand questions. Real demand requires both desire and money. A good's own price only slides buyers along the curve, whereas outside forces shift the entire curve. Finally, every elasticity puts quantity percentage on top and starts from the old values.

quickCheck.stem: (Practice) A consumer's monthly income rises from ₦50,000 to ₦60,000, and his monthly demand for garri falls from 40 cups to 36 cups. What is his income elasticity of demand, and what type of good is garri here?

options.why: This drops the minus sign; because quantity demanded fell when income rose, income elasticity is negative (−0.5), marking an inferior good.
This flips %ΔI over %ΔQ_{d}; income elasticity always places percentage change in quantity demanded in the numerator and income change in the denominator.
Complementary goods are identified by negative cross elasticity between two goods, whereas income elasticity classifies normal versus inferior goods.

steps.title: Yam in the barn versus yam at the stall
steps.display: Effective supply = Quantity offered for sale at a price and time (not total harvest)
working: Farmer harvests 300 yams, keeps 50 at home, brings 250 to sell.
Total production = 300  |  Effective supply = 250 tubers.
steps.narration: A farmer may dig three hundred tubers of yam from the soil. Only the tubers actually carried to the market stall for sale today count as supply.

steps.title: Effective supply and the law of supply
steps.display: Law of supply: P ↑ ⇒ Q_{s} ↑  and  P ↓ ⇒ Q_{s} ↓ (ceteris paribus)
working: Effective supply: willing, able and ready to offer for sale at a price and time.
Supply curve slopes upward from left to right because higher prices cover rising costs.
Total output exceeds effective supply whenever producers keep part for home use or storage.
steps.narration: Why do sellers bring out more stock when prices climb? Higher prices cover rising production costs and boost profit. Holding everything else equal, higher price brings larger quantity supplied. If yam doubles from one thousand to two thousand naira per tuber, farmers rush extra tubers to market.

steps.title: Change in quantity supplied versus change in supply
steps.display: Own price moves Q_{s} along S  |  Non-price costs or shocks shift S
working: Movement along S: expansion (P ↑, Q_{s} ↑) or contraction (P ↓, Q_{s} ↓).
Shift right (S → S_{1}): lower input costs, better technology, subsidies, good weather, more firms.
Shift left (S → S_{2}): higher wages or taxes, drought, pests, import bans on raw materials.
steps.narration: Just like demand, separate sliding along the curve from shifting the whole curve. Only the good's own price moves quantity supplied up or down the existing curve. Outside changes move the entire curve. Suppose diesel prices surge for haulage trucks. Bakers supply fewer loaves at every price, shifting supply leftward.

steps.title: Three types of supply and abnormal supply curves
steps.display: Types: Joint, Competitive, Composite  |  Abnormal: Fixed (vertical) and Backward-bending labour
working: Joint supply: one source gives multiple goods (palm oil, kernels, brooms).
Competitive supply: alternatives for one want (meat and fish; butter and margarine).
Composite supply: one good serves several uses (palm oil for food, soap, pomade).
Backward-bending labour supply: very high wages lead workers to choose more leisure.
steps.narration: Products share links on the selling side too. Harvesting palm trees yields palm oil, kernels, and brooms together, which shows joint supply. Abnormal curves break the upward rule. Above a very high wage, workers start trading work hours for rest, making the labour supply curve bend backward.

steps.title: Price elasticity of supply and its five types
steps.display: PES = \frac{%ΔQ_{s}}{%ΔP}  |  E_{s} > 1 (elastic), E_{s} < 1 (inelastic), E_{s} = 1 (unitary)
working: Extreme cases: E_{s} = 0 (vertical, fixed supply) and E_{s} = ∞ (horizontal, fixed price).
PES is normally positive because price and quantity supplied move in the same direction.
steps.narration: Price elasticity of supply measures how fast sellers expand output after a price rise. Suppose prices jump twenty percent and factories quickly boost output by thirty percent. Dividing thirty by twenty gives one point five zero, so supply is elastic. Fixed land has zero elasticity because nobody creates extra acres.

steps.title: Determinants and applications of supply elasticity
steps.display: Key determinants: Time horizon, storage ability, spare capacity, production cost, entry ease
working: Time: pre-harvest farm supply is inelastic; long-run industrial adjustment is elastic.
Storage and spare capacity let firms adjust stock or output quickly when price changes.
Applications: explains sharp farm price swings and shows who bears indirect taxes.
steps.narration: Time is the biggest driver of supply responsiveness. Before maize ripens, farmers cannot produce extra cobs quickly even if prices soar. Factories with idle machines or stocked warehouses respond much faster. This also guides tax policy, because less elastic sellers absorb more of a new unit tax.

steps.title: Extract initial values and find percentage change in quantity supplied
steps.display: Cement price rises from ₦4,000 to ₦5,000; Q_{s} rises from 200 to 220 bags. Find PES.
steps.narration: Let us work through a cement supply example step by step. Always begin by noting the starting price and starting quantity. Supply grew by twenty bags out of the original two hundred bags. That works out to a ten percent increase in quantity supplied.

steps.title: Calculate the percentage change in price
steps.narration: Next, turn the naira price jump into a percentage. Cement climbed by one thousand naira from its starting price of four thousand naira. Dividing one thousand by four thousand gives one quarter, or twenty five percent. Now both changes share the same percentage scale.

steps.title: Divide percentage changes and interpret the coefficient
steps.display: PES = \frac{+10%}{+25%} = 0.40  ⇒  Fairly inelastic supply (0 < 0.40 < 1)
working: Because 0.40 < 1, supply is inelastic: output responds weakly to the price rise.
steps.narration: Divide the ten percent quantity jump by the twenty five percent price jump. You get zero point four zero. Notice that price rose much faster than cement output could keep up. Because zero point four zero is under one, cement supply here is fairly inelastic.

steps.title: JAMB-style practice question
steps.display: (Practice) Palm oil price rises from ₦800 to ₦1,000 per litre, and Q_{s} rises from 400 to 600 litres. Find PES and its type. (a) 0.5, inelastic (b) 2.0, elastic (c) 2.0, perfectly elastic (d) 0.25, inelastic
working: Target: compute PES and classify it accurately.
steps.narration: Now try a practice question on palm oil supply. Before touching your calculator, notice something quick. Price moved up modestly, while quantity supplied leaped by half. That tells you right away that quantity responded strongly, so look out for an elasticity above one.

steps.title: Compute percentage changes in quantity supplied and price
working: Quantity gained 200 litres from 400 ⇒ +50%.
Price gained ₦200 from ₦800 ⇒ +25%.
steps.narration: Compute both percentages carefully using the starting values. Two hundred extra litres out of four hundred is a fifty percent jump in supply. Two hundred extra naira out of eight hundred is a twenty five percent price rise. Both numbers stay positive because supply rose with price.

steps.title: Compute PES and rule out misleading options
steps.display: PES = \frac{+50%}{+25%} = 2.0  ⇒  Elastic supply (2.0 > 1)
working: Rule out 0.5 (flips %ΔP over %ΔQ_{s}) and 0.25 (wrong denominator).
Rule out 2.0, perfectly elastic (perfectly elastic requires PES = ∞).
Correct answer: 2.0, elastic supply.
steps.narration: Dividing fifty percent by twenty five percent gives two point zero. Do not get tricked into calling two point zero perfectly elastic, because perfectly elastic means infinite responsiveness on a flat line. Also reject zero point five, which flips price onto the top. Two point zero simply means elastic supply.

steps.title: Total production vs effective supply, and movement vs shift
steps.display: Wrong: supply = total output  |  Right: supply = quantity offered for sale; only own P moves along S
working: Unsold yams kept at home are production, not effective supply.
Own price changes Q_{s} (movement along S); costs, taxes and weather shift S.
steps.narration: Two definitions trip up many candidates. First, total harvest is not supply unless all of it reaches the market for sale. Second, a rise in the good's own price only slides you upward along the same supply curve. Only non-price costs or shocks shift the whole curve.

steps.title: Elastic supply (E > 1) versus perfectly elastic supply (E = ∞)
steps.display: Wrong: calling PES = 3.0 perfectly elastic  |  Right: 1 < PES < ∞ is elastic; PES = ∞ is perfectly elastic
working: PES = 3.0 means elastic supply (finite percentage response > 1).
Perfectly elastic supply (PES = ∞) is a horizontal line at one fixed price.
steps.narration: Watch out for sloppy labels in tricky exam choices. Suppose you compute a finite number above one, like three. That supply is simply elastic, not perfectly elastic. Save perfectly elastic strictly for a horizontal line where elasticity reaches infinity.

steps.title: Backward-bending labour supply versus fixed supply
steps.display: Fixed supply: vertical line (E_{s} = 0)  |  Backward-bending labour: high wages cut hours worked
working: Fixed supply: quantity stays constant at every price (e.g. land or today's fresh fish).
Backward-bending labour supply: above high wage W_{1}, workers prefer leisure over extra hours.
steps.narration: Do not confuse the two abnormal supply shapes. A vertical line means quantity stays completely locked at every price, like land. By contrast, the backward-bending labour curve slopes upward at first, then turns inward. At very high pay, workers earn enough and choose extra leisure instead.

steps.title: Supply responds to price along the curve and time governs elasticity
steps.display: Effective supply (offered for sale)  |  Own P → Q_{s} moves  |  Costs and shocks → S shifts  |  PES = \frac{%ΔQ_{s}}{%ΔP}
working: Short-run and pre-harvest supply is inelastic; time and spare capacity make supply elastic.
steps.narration: Remember the core logic of supply for your exam. Supply counts only what producers bring to market. Own price slides sellers along the curve, while production costs and weather shift it. Finally, put quantity percentage over price percentage, and remember that time makes supply more elastic.

quickCheck.stem: (Practice) Before harvest, a sudden rise in the price of fresh maize barely increases the quantity brought to market. Why is supply inelastic in this period?

options.text: Producers cannot quickly grow and harvest extra maize in a short time
options.why: Time is a major determinant of supply elasticity; before harvest, crops are still maturing on the farm so supply remains inelastic regardless of price.

options.text: Maize is a Giffen good whose demand rises with price
options.why: Giffen goods explain abnormal consumer demand behaviour, not why farmers cannot quickly expand crop supply before harvest.

options.text: Consumers are unwilling to pay higher prices for food
options.why: Buyer willingness relates to demand, whereas price elasticity of supply measures how fast producers can adjust output.

options.text: Supply elasticity is infinite before harvest
options.why: Infinite elasticity means endless quantity can be supplied at one fixed price, the exact opposite of inelastic pre-harvest supply.

lessons.title: Price determination, equilibrium and price control

steps.title: Tug-of-war at the yam stall
steps.display: Buyers pull price down. Sellers push price up. Balance stops the tug.
steps.narration: Picture a busy yam market. Too few tubers bring a rush that lifts prices. Unsold heaps force sellers to cut prices until trays clear.

steps.title: Market and functions of the price system
steps.display: Price signals allocate goods, guide producers and replace barter
working: Free market: demand and supply jointly fix price
Signals: guides consumers' choices and producers' output
Incentive and rationing: motivates labour and rations scarce goods
steps.narration: Before money, barter needed two traders to want each other's goods. Today, price does the talking for us. When garri gets costly, shoppers buy less while farmers plant more. Notice how one figure tells everyone what to make and buy. Even wages and rent are prices in factor markets.

steps.title: Equilibrium, surplus and shortage
steps.display: At equilibrium, Q_{d} = Q_{s}
working: Above P_{e}: Q_{s} > Q_{d} ⇒ excess supply (surplus), price falls
Below P_{e}: Q_{d} > Q_{s} ⇒ excess demand (shortage), price rises
Self-correcting: market forces push P back to P_{e}
steps.narration: Markets settle where buyers and sellers agree on the same quantity. Suppose tomatoes balance at five hundred naira per basket. Charge seven hundred, and baskets pile up unsold, forcing sellers to cut prices. Charge three hundred, and buyers queue and bid prices back up. Market forces always pull toward balance.

steps.title: Solving linear demand and supply equations
steps.display: Q_{d} = a − bP,  Q_{s} = c + dP  ⇒  set Q_{d} = Q_{s}
working: Step 1: Equate a − bP = c + dP
Step 2: Group P terms to find equilibrium price P^{*}
Step 3: Substitute P^{*} into both equations to confirm Q^{*}
steps.narration: Sometimes JAMB gives equations instead of a table. Why equate them? Because balance means buyers and sellers want the exact same quantity. Imagine quantity demanded is fifty minus P and supply is ten plus P. Setting them equal gives two P equals forty, so price is twenty naira.

steps.title: How shifts in demand and supply move equilibrium
steps.display: Rightward shift increases demand or supply; leftward shift reduces it
working: Demand rises (S fixed): P^{*} rises, Q^{*} rises
Demand falls (S fixed): P^{*} falls, Q^{*} falls
Supply rises (D fixed): P^{*} falls, Q^{*} rises
Supply falls (D fixed): P^{*} rises, Q^{*} falls
Equal simultaneous increase in D and S: P^{*} unchanged, Q^{*} rises
steps.narration: What happens when incomes or farm costs change? Whole curves shift and break the old balance. For instance, good rains expand yam harvests, shifting supply right. More yams chase the same buyers, so price drops while sales grow. Watch how demand and supply shifts move price in opposite ways.

steps.title: Maximum price ceilings and minimum price floors
steps.display: Ceiling below P_{e} ⇒ shortage  |  Floor above P_{e} ⇒ surplus
working: Maximum price (ceiling): legal highest price, effective when P_{c} < P_{e}
Ceiling effects: excess demand (shortage), rationing, hoarding, black market
Minimum price (floor): legal lowest price, effective when P_{f} > P_{e}
Floor effects: excess supply (surplus), secret undercutting, unemployment for minimum wage
steps.narration: Governments sometimes block prices from reaching balance to protect buyers or farmers. A low cap on fuel keeps prices below balance, creating queues and black markets. Conversely, a high floor price for cocoa leaves sacks unsold. High wage floors can also cause unemployment.

steps.title: Equate demand and supply functions
working: At equilibrium: Q_{d} = Q_{s}
steps.narration: Let us solve a full market problem step by step. Here are linear demand and supply rules for rice, with price in naira. Market balance requires buyers and sellers to match. So we set quantity demanded equal to quantity supplied.

steps.title: Solve for equilibrium price P*
steps.narration: Next, gather numbers on one side and price terms on the other. Moving minus four P across turns it into plus four P, giving ten P. Moving twenty left leaves eighty. Dividing eighty by ten gives an equilibrium price of eight naira per bag.

steps.title: Find and verify equilibrium quantity Q*
steps.display: Q^{*} = 68 bags
steps.narration: Do not stop at price. Plug eight naira back into the demand rule to get thirty two subtracted from one hundred, which is sixty eight. Check the supply rule too. Twenty plus forty eight also equals sixty eight, proving our algebra is right.

steps.title: Find the shortage under a ₦5 price ceiling
steps.display: At P = ₦5:  shortage = Q_{d} − Q_{s} = 30 bags
working: Excess demand = 80 − 50 = 30 bags
steps.narration: Now suppose government caps the rice price at five naira. Since five is below eight, buyers want eighty bags while sellers offer only fifty. Subtracting fifty from eighty shows a shortage of thirty bags. Keep that gap formula in mind for exam calculations.

steps.title: JAMB-style practice question
steps.display: (Practice) Cheaper fertiliser lowers maize production cost while tastes stay unchanged. What happens to equilibrium price and quantity?
working: A. Price rises, quantity falls
B. Price falls, quantity rises
C. Both price and quantity rise
D. Price stays unchanged, quantity rises
steps.narration: Here is a practice question on market shifts. First ask which curve moves. Cheaper fertiliser cuts farmers' production costs, making maize more profitable to grow at every price. Tastes and incomes did not change, so only the supply curve shifts to the right.

steps.title: Trace the new equilibrium
steps.display: Supply shifts right (S → S_{1}) along fixed demand D
working: At old P_{0}: Q_{s} > Q_{d} (temporary surplus)
Surplus pushes price down from P_{0} to P_{1}
Lower price expands quantity demanded from Q_{0} to Q_{1}
steps.narration: See what happens at the original price once supply expands. Farmers bring more maize than shoppers want at that old price. Unsold bags create a temporary surplus, pushing the price down. As price falls, buyers purchase more, so equilibrium settles at lower price and higher quantity.

steps.title: Rule out the distractors
steps.display: Correct answer: Price falls, quantity rises
working: Price rises, quantity falls: that comes from a decrease in supply
Both rise: that comes from an increase in demand
Price unchanged: happens only if D and S rise equally
steps.narration: Let us rule out the wrong choices one by one. Higher price with lower quantity happens only when supply shrinks, not grows. Both rising requires a demand boom. An unchanged price needs an equal rise in both curves. Only falling price with rising quantity fits.

steps.title: Do not swap price floor and price ceiling
steps.display: Wrong  Price floor ⇒ shortage  |  Right  Price floor above P_{e} ⇒ surplus
working: Binding ceiling (below P_{e}): Q_{d} > Q_{s} ⇒ shortage
Binding floor (above P_{e}): Q_{s} > Q_{d} ⇒ surplus
Non-binding control (ceiling > P_{e} or floor < P_{e}): no effect
steps.narration: Many students see the word floor and picture a low price causing queues. In fact, a binding floor sits above balance to stop prices dropping further. High prices tempt sellers to bring extra goods while buyers cut back, leaving a surplus. Remember, ceilings cause shortages.

steps.title: Supply increase lowers price, never raises it
steps.display: Wrong  S rises ⇒ P^{*} rises  |  Right  S rises ⇒ P^{*} falls, Q^{*} rises
working: Supply shifts right: more goods at every price
Excess supply at old P^{*} forces price down to clear stock
steps.narration: Students often confuse an increase in supply with an increase in demand because both boost quantity sold. Yet their price effects point in opposite directions. More demand lets sellers charge higher prices. More supply floods the stalls, so sellers must cut prices to clear stock.

steps.title: Check signs and verify both equations
steps.display: Wrong  100 − 4P = 20 + 6P ⇒ 2P = 80  |  Right  10P = 80
working: Adding 4P to both sides gives 6P + 4P = 10P, not 6P − 4P
Always plug P^{*} into both Q_{d} and Q_{s} to confirm they match
steps.narration: Rushing algebra costs easy marks in equilibrium problems. When you move minus four P across the equals sign, its sign flips to plus, giving ten P rather than two P. Always substitute your price back into both equations. If the quantities disagree, recheck your signs immediately.

steps.title: Price balances the market unless blocked
steps.display: Q_{d} = Q_{s} clears the market; shifts move it; controls lock in gaps
steps.narration: Keep this single picture in your head. Left alone, market price moves until demand equals supply, clearing every stall. Shifts in demand or supply move that balance point. When government laws hold price below balance, shortages appear. When laws hold price above balance, surpluses pile up.

quickCheck.stem: (Practice) The demand and supply equations for garri are Q_{d} = 80 − 2P and Q_{s} = 20 + 4P. If the government enforces a minimum price of ₦15, what is the market outcome?

options.why: A shortage occurs only when a price ceiling is set below equilibrium, whereas ₦15 is above the equilibrium price of ₦10.
Equilibrium is at P^{*} = ₦10 (80 − 2P = 20 + 4P ⇒ 6P = 60). At the ₦15 floor, Q_{s} = 80 and Q_{d} = 50, giving a surplus of 30 units.
60 units is the equilibrium quantity at P^{*} = ₦10, which cannot hold when a binding minimum price forces price up to ₦15.
50 units is the quantity demanded at ₦15 (80 − 2 × 15), not the excess supply gap Q_{s} − Q_{d}.

lessons.title: Production, factors of production and the law of diminishing returns

steps.title: Crowding the bread oven
steps.display: Adding hands speeds up baking until workers crowd one oven
steps.narration: One baker mixes, bakes, and sells slowly. Adding two helpers multiplies daily loaves fast. Pack ten helpers around one small oven, and they bump elbows while loaves drop.

steps.title: Meaning, types and stages of production
steps.display: Production creates utility until goods reach final consumers
working: Types: direct (for own or family use) vs indirect (for sale or exchange)
Primary: extracting raw materials (farming, fishing, mining)
Secondary: processing into finished goods (manufacturing, construction)
Tertiary: distribution and services (transport, banking, teaching)
steps.narration: Production does not end at the factory gate. It means creating usefulness, and it finishes only when buyers receive the item. Think of crude oil or cocoa. Extracting cocoa is primary, turning it into chocolate is secondary, and trucking or banking the trade is tertiary. Subsistence farms use direct production.

steps.title: Four factors of production and their rewards
steps.display: Land → Rent  |  Labour → Wages  |  Capital → Interest  |  Entrepreneur → Profit
working: Land: free gift of nature, fixed supply in long run, immobile
Labour: human physical and mental effort, mobile, cannot be stored
Capital: man-made wealth for further production (fixed, working, or social)
Entrepreneur: organises other factors, makes decisions, bears risk (profit or loss)
steps.narration: Every business combines four distinct inputs. On a rice farm, soil and water are land earning rent. Farmhands supply human effort for wages. Tractors and seeds are man-made capital earning interest. The owner risks money and organises everyone else, earning profit when sales beat costs, or bearing loss.

steps.title: Division of labour and specialisation
steps.display: Splitting production into tasks boosts skill and output, limited by market size
working: Merits: saves time, raises skill and output, allows mechanisation, cuts unit cost
Demerits: monotony, loss of craft skill, machine displacement, interdependence
Key limit: division of labour is limited by the extent of the market
steps.narration: Why do workers split tasks instead of one person doing everything? Splitting a job saves switching time and sharpens skill through practice. In a modern bakery, one person mixes dough, another moulds loaves, and another runs the oven. However, tiny villages cannot sustain narrow specialists because demand is too small.

steps.title: Internal vs external economies of scale
steps.display: Large scale lowers unit cost; over-expansion causes diseconomies
working: Internal economies (own firm grows): technical, marketing, financial, managerial, research, risk-bearing
External economies (industry or estate clusters): shared roads, skilled labour pool, specialised suppliers
Diseconomies: bureaucracy and poor supervision (internal) or crowding and congestion (external)
steps.narration: Growing larger cuts average cost per item in two ways. First, a huge bottling plant buys crates in bulk and borrows cheaply on its own size. Second, workshops clustered in one industrial estate share good roads and trained technicians. Grow too big, though, and red tape or traffic pushes costs back up.

steps.title: Total, Average and Marginal Product
steps.display: AP = \frac{TP}{L},  MP = \frac{ΔTP}{ΔL}
working: Total Product (TP): total output produced (TP = AP × L)
Average Product (AP): output per worker
Marginal Product (MP): extra output from one more worker
Key link: TP peaks where MP = 0; TP falls when MP < 0
steps.narration: Economists track short-run output with three numbers. Total product counts every bag made. Dividing total bags by workers gives average output per worker. Marginal product tracks only the extra bags brought by the newest hire. If four workers harvest sixty bags and a fifth adds five, marginal product is five.

steps.title: The Law of Diminishing Returns (Variable Proportions)
steps.display: Adding variable input to a fixed factor eventually lowers MP
working: Short-run law: at least one factor (e.g. land) stays fixed
Stage 1: MP rises at first as teamwork improves
Stage 2: MP falls (still positive) ⇒ TP rises more slowly
Stage 3: MP turns negative (< 0) ⇒ TP falls due to overcrowding
steps.narration: In the short run, farm land or shop space stays fixed while you hire more hands. Imagine adding weavers to just two looms. Early hires boost extra output through teamwork. Soon looms get crowded, so each extra hire adds less than the previous one. Eventually, crowding actually shrinks total cloth.

steps.title: Calculate Average Product (AP)
steps.display: Fixed land: 1 hectare  |  L = 1..6  |  TP = 10, 26, 45, 60, 60, 54 bags
working: At L = 4: AP = \frac{60}{4} = 15 bags per worker
At L = 6: AP = \frac{54}{6} = 9 bags per worker
steps.narration: Let us work through a maize farm table with one fixed hectare. We want average product, marginal product, and the point of diminishing returns. First, divide total output by the number of workers. Four workers making sixty bags average fifteen each, whereas six workers making fifty four average nine.

steps.title: Calculate Marginal Product (MP)
steps.display: MP = \frac{TP_{n} − TP_{n−1}}{L_{n} − L_{n−1}}
steps.narration: Now measure what each extra worker adds on top of the previous total. Moving from one to two workers raises output by sixteen bags. The third worker adds nineteen bags. Watch closely from the fourth onward. The fourth adds fifteen, the fifth adds zero, and the sixth drops output by six.

steps.title: Spot where diminishing returns set in
steps.display: Diminishing marginal returns begin after the 3rd worker
working: MP rises from 10 (L = 1) → 16 (L = 2) → 19 (L = 3)
At L = 4, MP drops from 19 to 15
steps.narration: Where does diminishing marginal return begin? Look for the highest marginal product, not the highest total product. Extra output climbs through the third hire, peaking at nineteen bags. Because the fourth hire adds only fifteen bags, diminishing returns set in right after the third worker.

steps.title: Verify maximum TP and negative MP
steps.display: Max TP = 60 bags (MP = 0 at L = 5);  TP falls at L = 6 (MP = −6)
working: Total output peaks at 60 bags when MP reaches 0
Adding a 6th worker causes overcrowding: TP falls to 54, MP = −6
steps.narration: Check how total and marginal numbers stay linked at the end. At the fifth worker, extra output hits zero. Total harvest stands at its sixty-bag peak right there. Hiring a sixth worker crowds the plot. Marginal output turns negative, pulling total harvest down.

steps.title: JAMB-style practice question
steps.display: (Practice) A large textile mill buys raw cotton in bulk at discounts and gets cheaper bank loans than small mills. This illustrates
working: A. external economies of scale
B. internal economies of scale
C. diminishing marginal returns
D. tertiary production
steps.narration: Try this practice question on scale of production. Notice what causes the savings here. The mill gets cheaper cotton and cheaper loans simply because of its own large size, not because other mills moved next door. Keep that distinction in mind before looking at the choices.

steps.title: Match the two cost advantages
steps.display: Bulk buying = marketing economy  |  Cheaper loans = financial economy
working: Both arise from the firm's own expansion of scale
Therefore both are internal economies of scale
steps.narration: Now name each cost saving from the textbook list. Buying raw cotton in bulk at lower prices is a marketing economy. Securing bank credit at lower interest rates is a financial economy. Because both spring from one firm's own growth, they belong under internal economies of scale.

steps.title: Eliminate the wrong options
steps.display: Correct answer: internal economies of scale
working: External economies come from industry clustering, not own size
Diminishing returns is a short-run rise in cost from fixed factors
Textile manufacturing is secondary, not tertiary production
steps.narration: Let us eliminate the remaining traps. External savings come from many firms clustering in an industrial zone, not one firm's own size. Diminishing returns describes falling extra output in the short run. Finally, weaving cotton into cloth is secondary manufacturing, not tertiary service delivery.

steps.title: Falling MP does not mean falling TP right away
steps.display: Wrong  MP falls ⇒ TP falls  |  Right  MP > 0 ⇒ TP still rises (slower)
working: When MP drops from 19 to 15, TP still climbs from 45 to 60
TP only drops when MP becomes negative (< 0)
steps.narration: Students often hear diminishing returns and assume total output drops right away. Look at the numbers again. When the fourth worker adds fifteen instead of nineteen, total bags still rise from forty five to sixty. Total output falls only after marginal product drops below zero.

steps.title: Keep internal and external economies separate
steps.display: Wrong  Shared estate roads = internal  |  Right  Shared estate benefits = external
working: Internal: firm's own expansion (bulk buying, own research lab, own bank credit)
External: industry location and growth (shared estate infrastructure, pool of skilled workers)
steps.narration: Both economies lower average cost, so JAMB loves swapping them. Ask one quick test question. Did the firm earn this saving by growing bigger itself, or by sitting near rival firms? Own size means internal. Shared roads, suppliers, or trained workers in an estate mean external.

steps.title: Do not merge entrepreneur with labour or swap rewards
steps.display: Wrong  Entrepreneur earns wages  |  Right  Entrepreneur bears risk for profit
working: Land → Rent;  Labour → Wages and Salaries;  Capital → Interest
Entrepreneur is separated from labour because only the entrepreneur bears business risk and organises production
steps.narration: Since entrepreneurs work hard daily, students sometimes lump them under labour. Economists keep them separate for a clear reason. Ordinary workers earn agreed wages without risking business capital. Only the entrepreneur coordinates the firm, makes key decisions, and takes profit or loss.

steps.title: Combine factors well, scale wisely, watch fixed limits
steps.display: Four factors create utility; scale cuts unit cost until fixed inputs bind
steps.narration: Production creates usefulness and ends only when goods reach buyers. Four rewarded factors power that chain. Specialisation and larger scale drive unit costs down. Yet whenever one factor stays fixed in the short run, adding too many variable inputs brings diminishing returns.

quickCheck.stem: (Practice) On a fixed plot of land, 4 workers produce 80 bags of cassava, 5 workers produce 95 bags, and 6 workers produce 90 bags. What is the marginal product of the 6th worker?

options.why: 15 bags is the marginal product of the 5th worker (95 − 80), not the 6th worker.
Marginal product is ΔTP ÷ ΔL = (90 − 95) ÷ (6 − 5) = −5 bags; total product falls when MP turns negative.
19 bags is the average product of 5 workers (95 ÷ 5), whereas marginal product measures the change in total product.
Total product dropped from 95 to 90 bags when the 6th worker joined, so the marginal product must carry a minus sign (−5).

lessons.title: Costs and revenue (fixed, variable, average, marginal)

steps.title: Shop rent versus daily pure-water stock
steps.display: Shop rent (paid even with zero sales) + stock bought = total cost  |  Sales cash = total revenue
working: Fixed bill stays the same whether you sell zero bags or fifty.
Stock bill rises with every extra bag of pure water you buy.
steps.narration: Picture a Nigerian roadside kiosk. You pay shop rent even when nobody buys. Ice and pure water only cost money as sales grow. That splits fixed from variable.

steps.title: Accountant's money cost versus economist's opportunity cost
steps.display: Accounting cost = explicit money paid  |  Economic cost = explicit cost + implicit (opportunity) cost
working: Accountant counts actual cash spent on wages, rent, and materials (money cost).
Economist counts real cost: the next best alternative foregone, including owner's foregone pay.
Accounting profit = TR − explicit cost  |  Economic profit = TR − (explicit + implicit cost)
steps.narration: Accountants track receipts leaving the till. Economists also value what you gave up to run the shop. Suppose a barber quits a twenty thousand naira job to open a salon. His accountant ignores that lost salary. The economist counts it as real cost.

steps.title: Total fixed cost, total variable cost, and total cost
steps.display: TC = TFC + TVC  |  At Q = 0, TVC = 0 and TC = TFC
working: TFC (fixed cost): constant in the short run regardless of output (rent, heavy machinery, top salaries).
TVC (variable cost): rises directly with output (raw materials, piece-rate labour, fuel used in production).
Total cost (TC) sums all fixed and variable outlays at each output level.
steps.narration: Some bills never budge when output pauses. Others climb with every unit made. Together they form total cost. Think of a garri processor paying ten thousand naira monthly rent for the shed. Even at zero output she pays rent. Cassava and firewood rise with each bag.

steps.title: Average cost curves: AFC, AVC, and ATC
steps.display: AFC = \frac{TFC}{Q}  |  AVC = \frac{TVC}{Q}  |  ATC = \frac{TC}{Q} = AFC + AVC
working: AFC falls continuously as Q increases because fixed cost is spread over more units.
AVC and ATC are U-shaped: they fall at first, then rise as diminishing returns set in.
ATC always lies above AVC by the vertical gap AFC, and narrows toward AVC at high output.
steps.narration: Managers need cost per unit to set sensible prices. Dividing fixed cost by output shrinks steadily as volume grows. Variable cost per unit first dips, then climbs once workers crowd the machine. Imagine sharing a twelve hundred naira generator bill across two cakes versus six cakes.

steps.title: Marginal cost and its link to averages and supply
steps.display: MC = \frac{Δ TC}{Δ Q} = \frac{Δ TVC}{Δ Q}  |  MC cuts AVC and ATC at their minima
working: Because TFC is constant in the short run, any change in TC equals the change in TVC.
When MC < AC, AC falls; when MC > AC, AC rises; when MC = AC, AC is at its minimum.
For a competitive firm, the upward-sloping MC curve above minimum AVC serves as its supply curve.
steps.narration: Marginal cost asks one sharp question. How much extra does one more unit cost to make? If the next loaf costs less than your current average, the average drops. Once it costs more, the average climbs. Say three loaves average five hundred naira. Baking a fourth for nine hundred pulls the average up.

steps.title: Short-run versus long-run cost horizons
steps.display: Short run: at least one fixed factor (TFC > 0)  |  Long run: all factors variable (no fixed costs)
working: Short run: output can rise only by adding variable inputs (labour, materials) to fixed plant and land.
Long run: all inputs, including machinery and buildings, can be varied to match demand.
In the long run, every cost is variable (TC = TVC).
steps.narration: Time changes what a firm can adjust. Today a bakery cannot magically double its oven space, so fixed costs stay locked in. Give the owner a year, and she can move to a larger building. Picture a tailor stuck with one shop lease for six months before expanding.

steps.title: Revenue concepts and profit calculation
steps.display: TR = P × Q  |  AR = \frac{TR}{Q} = P  |  MR = \frac{Δ TR}{Δ Q}  |  Profit = TR − TC
working: Total revenue (TR) is total sales income earned from selling Q units.
Average revenue (AR) equals revenue per unit sold, which is identical to unit price P.
Marginal revenue (MR) is the extra revenue from selling one additional unit.
steps.narration: Costs are only half the story. Revenue tracks money coming in from buyers. Average revenue simply tells you the selling price per unit. Marginal revenue tracks the extra cash from one more sale. Suppose selling three shirts brings sixty naira, and four shirts bring seventy five. The fourth shirt adds fifteen naira marginal revenue.

steps.title: Build Total Cost from fixed and variable costs
steps.display: Sachet-water plant: TFC = ₦1,200. TVC at Q = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 batches is ₦0, ₦600, ₦1,000, ₦1,500, ₦2,400. Find AFC, AVC, ATC, and MC at Q = 3 and Q = 4.
working: TC = TFC + TVC at every batch:
steps.narration: Let us work through a sachet water plant schedule together. Fixed cost stays at one thousand two hundred naira for every row. Add variable cost to get total cost at each batch. Notice we also compute batch two because we need it next for marginal cost.

steps.title: Compute AFC, AVC, and ATC at Q = 3 and Q = 4
steps.display: Divide TFC, TVC, and TC by Q  |  Verify ATC = AFC + AVC
steps.narration: Now divide each total by the batch number. At three batches, average fixed cost is four hundred naira and average variable cost is five hundred. Together they give nine hundred. Watch average fixed cost drop to three hundred at four batches while average variable cost climbs to six hundred.

steps.title: Calculate Marginal Cost and spot the crossing points
steps.display: MC = \frac{Δ TC}{Δ Q}  |  At Q = 3: MC = AVC = ₦500  |  At Q = 4: MC = ATC = ₦900
working: Notice MC equals minimum AVC (₦500) at Q = 3 and minimum ATC (₦900) at Q = 4.
steps.narration: To get marginal cost, subtract the previous total cost from the new one. Moving from two to three adds five hundred naira, which matches average variable cost at its lowest. Moving to four adds nine hundred, matching average total cost right at its bottom. Keep those crossing points in mind.

steps.title: JAMB-style practice question on revenue and economic cost
steps.display: (Practice) A tailor buys fabric and pays helpers ₦18,000, pays ₦12,000 shop rent, and sells 10 dresses at ₦4,500 each. She gave up a ₦20,000 monthly wage to run the shop. Find her accounting profit and economic profit.
working: Implicit (opportunity) cost = ₦20,000 foregone salary
steps.narration: Here is a practice question testing revenue alongside both cost viewpoints. First find total revenue by multiplying ten dresses by four thousand five hundred naira. Next separate cash paid out from the salary she gave up. Cash bills total thirty thousand naira, while the missed wage is twenty thousand.

steps.title: Compute accounting profit from explicit money costs
steps.display: Accounting profit = TR − Explicit cost = ₦45,000 − ₦30,000 = ₦15,000
working: Total Revenue = ₦45,000
Total Explicit Cost = ₦30,000
Accounting profit = ₦45,000 − ₦30,000 = ₦15,000
steps.narration: An accountant looks strictly at cash received minus cash spent. Forty five thousand naira in sales minus thirty thousand naira in fabric, wages, and rent leaves fifteen thousand naira. On paper the shop looks profitable. Wait before celebrating, because we have not checked her missed job yet.

steps.title: Include implicit cost to find economic profit
working: Economic cost = Explicit cost + Implicit cost = ₦30,000 + ₦20,000 = ₦50,000
Economic profit = ₦45,000 − ₦50,000 = −₦5,000 (an economic loss of ₦5,000)
steps.narration: Now think like an economist and include the twenty thousand naira salary she sacrificed. Total economic cost reaches fifty thousand naira. Subtracting fifty thousand from forty five thousand leaves minus five thousand. She made an accounting profit yet suffered an economic loss of five thousand naira.

steps.title: Confusing fixed costs with essential variable inputs
steps.display: Wrong: Cotton in a textile mill is fixed because it is essential  |  Right: Cotton varies with cloth woven, so it is TVC
working: Apply the zero-output test: if Q = 0 requires ₦0 of the input, it is a variable cost.
Raw materials (cotton, cassava, flour) and piece-rate wages are variable costs; rent and machinery are fixed.
steps.narration: Students often call raw materials fixed costs just because a factory cannot run without them. That is the wrong test. Ask what happens when production stops for a week. You still pay shop rent, so rent is fixed. You buy zero cotton, so cotton is variable.

steps.title: Treating money cost as economist's cost
steps.display: Wrong: Opportunity cost = cash paid  |  Right: Money cost = cash paid; Opportunity cost = next best alternative foregone
working: Accountant's cost counts explicit cash payments only.
Economist's cost includes explicit payments plus implicit opportunity costs (self-owned shop, foregone salary).
steps.narration: Another classic exam trap mixes up money cost and opportunity cost. Cash printed on a receipt is money cost. Opportunity cost measures the single best alternative you sacrificed. Even when you own your own shop building, giving up rental income from a tenant is an implicit economic cost.

steps.title: Dividing TC by Q for MC, or missing the minimum-AC crossing
steps.display: Wrong: MC = \frac{TC}{Q}  |  Right: MC = \frac{Δ TC}{Δ Q}, and MC cuts AVC and ATC at their minima
working: \frac{TC}{Q} gives Average Total Cost (ATC), never Marginal Cost (MC).
Always check Δ Q: if Q jumps by 2 units, divide Δ TC by 2, not 1.
steps.narration: Never divide total cost by total quantity when asked for marginal cost. That formula gives average cost instead. Marginal cost always uses the change in total cost divided by the change in output. Also remember that marginal cost cuts both average variable and average total cost at their lowest points.

steps.title: Split fixed from variable, watch the margin, and count opportunity cost
steps.display: TC = TFC + TVC  |  ATC = AFC + AVC  |  MC = \frac{Δ TC}{Δ Q} cuts AVC & ATC at minima  |  Profit = TR − TC
working: Economist's cost = explicit money cost + implicit opportunity cost.
TR = P × Q, AR = P, and MR = \frac{Δ TR}{Δ Q}; in the long run all costs are variable.
steps.narration: Keep three habits sharp for every cost and revenue question. First, separate fixed bills from variable ones, knowing all inputs become variable in the long run. Second, use changes for marginal cost and marginal revenue, and remember marginal cost cuts average curves at their minima. Finally, always count opportunity cost.

quickCheck.stem: (Practice) A firm's total fixed cost is ₦600. When output rises from 2 units to 3 units, total cost increases from ₦1,000 to ₦1,500. What are the marginal cost (MC) of the 3rd unit and the average variable cost (AVC) at 3 units?

options.why: ₦500 is the Average Total Cost (TC ÷ Q = \frac{1,500}{3}), not AVC. You must subtract TFC = ₦600 first to get TVC = ₦900.
₦1,500 is Total Cost at 3 units, not the extra (marginal) cost of adding the 3rd unit (1,500 − 1,000 = ₦500).
This swaps AVC (₦300) into MC and gives AFC (\frac{600}{3} = ₦200) instead of AVC.

steps.title: Many garri stalls versus one borehole vendor
steps.display: Balogun garri stalls: many sellers, one ruling price  |  Lone borehole vendor: single seller sets the price
working: When dozens of traders sell identical garri side by side, no single seller can raise the price.
When one supplier owns the only borehole in an area, buyers must accept the price set.
steps.narration: Think of Balogun market where dozens sell identical garri at one ruling price. Contrast that with a lone borehole owner in a new estate who sets the price.

steps.title: Perfect competition: assumptions and price-taking
steps.display: Price taker: P = AR = MR (horizontal demand curve)
working: Many buyers and sellers, each too small to influence market price.
Homogeneous (identical) goods, free entry and exit, perfect knowledge of market prices.
