Free mobility of factors, no preferential treatment, and a single ruling market price.
steps.narration: In perfect competition, market supply and demand fix one price that every firm accepts. Goods are identical, and buyers know every stall's price. Picture forty rice stalls selling the exact same grain at ten thousand naira per bag. Raise yours to eleven thousand, and shoppers walk away.

steps.title: Short-run and long-run equilibrium in perfect competition
steps.display: Short run: P = MC = MR (abnormal profit, normal profit, or loss)  |  Long run: P = AC = AR = MC = MR
working: Profit is maximised (or loss minimised) where MC = MR and MC is rising.
Short run: abnormal profit if P > AC, or loss if P < AC.
Long run: free entry wipes out abnormal profit and exit wipes out loss, leaving only normal profit at minimum AC.
steps.narration: Every firm picks output where marginal cost meets marginal revenue. In the short run, high demand brings extra profits. Suppose pure water sellers earn fat profits this month. Soon new rivals enter, supply jumps, and price drops until only normal profit remains at lowest average cost.

steps.title: Pure monopoly: causes, price-making, and equilibrium
steps.display: Price maker: P = AR > MR (downward-sloping)  |  Equilibrium: MC = MR with P > MC
working: Single seller of a commodity with no close substitute and strong barriers to entry.
Causes: natural resource control, Act of Parliament, patents or copyrights, mergers, superior technology.
Because demand slopes downward, selling more lowers price on all units, so MR lies below AR (P > MC).
steps.narration: A pure monopolist is the sole seller with no close substitute. Barriers like patents or state statutes block rivals. To sell extra units, the firm must cut price on all units, so marginal revenue sits below price. Think of a sole power utility choosing output where marginal curves meet.

steps.title: Discriminatory monopoly and monopolistic competition
steps.display: Discriminatory monopoly: different prices across separated markets  |  Monopolistic competition: many sellers, differentiated goods
working: Discriminatory monopoly charges different prices for the same product when resale between groups is prevented.
Monopolistic competition blends competition (many firms, free entry) with monopoly power (product differentiation).
Under monopolistic competition, short-run profit is possible (P > MC = MR), while long-run entry restores normal profit (P = AC) with excess capacity.
steps.narration: Not all imperfect markets are single sellers. A discriminatory monopolist charges different prices to separated buyer groups, like cheaper student bus tickets. Meanwhile, monopolistic competition fills real markets with many branded sellers. Imagine ten neighbourhood bakeries selling slightly different bread loaves, earning only normal profit over time.

steps.title: Break-even point versus short-run shut-down point
steps.display: Break-even: P = AC (TR = TC)  |  Operate at loss: AVC < P < AC  |  Short-run shut-down: P < AVC (TR < TVC)
working: At P = AC (TR = TC), the firm breaks even and earns zero economic profit (normal profit).
If AVC < P < AC, revenue covers all variable cost and helps pay part of fixed cost, so keep producing in the short run.
If P < AVC (TR < TVC), producing adds variable losses to fixed cost, so shut down immediately; in the long run, exit whenever P < AC.
steps.narration: When prices slump, managers ask two distinct questions. Breaking even means price covers total unit cost. Shutting down immediately only makes sense if price falls below average variable cost. Suppose a tailor pays five thousand naira rent and spends three thousand on cloth. Earning four thousand still shrinks her loss.

steps.title: Merits, demerits, and government control of monopoly
steps.display: Merits: economies of scale, R&D, no duplication  |  Demerits: high P, low Q, inefficiency  |  Control: privatisation, imports, regulation
working: Advantages: large-scale lower unit cost (natural monopoly), avoids duplicate cables or pipes, encourages invention via patents.
Disadvantages: higher prices, restricted output (artificial scarcity), consumer exploitation, inefficiency, less choice.
Controls: privatisation, tariff cuts to allow import competition, banning mergers, ending monopoly laws or patents, price and output regulation.
steps.narration: Society weighs monopoly benefits against consumer harm. One water utility avoids digging duplicate street pipes and lowers unit cost. Yet unchecked monopolies raise prices, restrict output, and grow lazy. Think of government opening telecoms to private rivals or cutting import tariffs to force prices down.

steps.title: Find total revenue, total cost, and operating profit or loss
steps.display: A competitive firm has TFC = ₦1,000 and price P = ₦300. At MC = MR output Q = 5 units, TVC = ₦1,200. Should it operate or shut down in the short run?
working: Operating profit = TR − TC = ₦1,500 − ₦2,200 = −₦700 (a loss of ₦700)
steps.narration: Let us test the shut down decision with real numbers. First calculate total revenue and total cost at five units. Revenue is one thousand five hundred naira, while total cost is two thousand two hundred. Running the shop gives a seven hundred naira loss.

steps.title: Compare price against AVC and ATC
working: AVC = \frac{TVC}{Q} = \frac{1,200}{5} = ₦240 per unit
ATC = \frac{TC}{Q} = \frac{2,200}{5} = ₦440 per unit
Since P = ₦300 exceeds AVC = ₦240, each unit contributes ₦60 toward fixed cost.
steps.narration: Next check unit costs instead of guessing from the total loss. Variable cost per unit is two hundred and forty naira. That sits below the three hundred naira selling price. So each unit pays its variable bill and leaves sixty naira toward rent.

steps.title: Compare operating loss against shut-down loss
steps.display: Operating loss = ₦700 < Shut-down loss (TFC) = ₦1,000  →  Keep operating in the short run
working: If Q = 0 (shut down), TR = ₦0 and TVC = ₦0, so loss equals TFC = ₦1,000.
Operating cuts the loss from ₦1,000 down to ₦700 (saving ₦300).
Decision: continue operating in the short run; exit in the long run if P remains below ATC (₦440).
steps.narration: Compare the two losses side by side. Closing today leaves zero sales and a full one thousand naira rent loss. Staying open cuts that loss to seven hundred naira. So keep producing now, and close later if low prices persist.

steps.title: JAMB-style practice question on monopoly equilibrium
steps.display: (Practice) A monopolist faces demand: Q = 1 at P = ₦100, Q = 2 at P = ₦90, Q = 3 at P = ₦80, and Q = 4 at P = ₦70. If MC = ₦60 per unit and the firm produces up to MC = MR, find equilibrium output and price.
steps.narration: Now try a practice question on how a monopolist sets price and quantity. Unlike a competitive seller, cutting price to sell more lowers revenue on earlier units too. Multiply price by quantity for total revenue, then subtract row by row for marginal revenue. Watch how quickly marginal revenue falls.

steps.title: Apply the MC = MR rule to choose output
working: Units 1 and 2 have MR (₦100, ₦80) > MC (₦60), so expanding output raises profit.
At Q = 3, MR = ₦60 equals MC = ₦60.
Unit 4 adds only ₦40 in revenue while costing ₦60, so never produce Q = 4.
steps.narration: Next match marginal revenue against the sixty naira marginal cost. The first two units bring in more than sixty naira, so keep producing. The third unit brings sixty naira, matching cost right on the button. Stop there, because unit four adds forty while costing sixty.

steps.title: Read monopoly price from the demand schedule
steps.display: Equilibrium output Q = 3 units  |  Monopoly price P = ₦80 (> MC = ₦60)
working: At Q = 3 units, the demand schedule (AR) shows buyers will pay P = ₦80.
Notice the hallmark of monopoly: MC = MR (₦60) determines Q = 3, while demand gives P = ₦80 > MC.
steps.narration: Do not confuse marginal cost with the monopoly price. Marginal cost equals marginal revenue at three units, giving the output decision. Then look up at the demand table to see what buyers pay for three units. That sets the price at eighty naira, comfortably above sixty.

steps.title: Confusing government barriers with natural or capital barriers
steps.display: Wrong: High start-up costs are created by government  |  Right: Patents, copyrights, and licences are legal government barriers
working: Legal and government barriers: Acts of Parliament, patents, copyrights, and statutory licences.
Natural and economic barriers: economies of scale, high start-up capital, raw material control, brand loyalty.
steps.narration: Exam questions often ask which barrier comes from government action. High start up capital and economies of scale happen naturally in heavy industry without any law. Patents, copyrights, and state charters exist only because government laws create and enforce them.

steps.title: Thinking a monopolist equates P = MC or never loses money
steps.display: Wrong: Monopolist sets P = MC and always profits  |  Right: Monopolist sets MC = MR (so P > MC) and loses if AC > P
working: Only a price-taking perfect competitor has P = AR = MR = MC in equilibrium.
A monopolist has P = AR > MR = MC, and still makes a loss whenever AC lies above demand (P < AC).
steps.narration: Two monopoly myths trip students up fast. First, a monopolist never sets price equal to marginal cost, because price sits above marginal revenue. Second, monopoly power does not guarantee profit. When weak demand pushes average total cost above the demand curve, even a sole seller loses money.

steps.title: Confusing the break-even point with the short-run shut-down point
steps.display: Wrong: Shut down whenever P < AC  |  Right: P = AC is break-even; short-run shut-down is P < AVC
working: Break-even point: P = AC (TR = TC), zero economic profit.
If AVC < P < AC, staying open covers variable cost and reduces fixed-cost loss.
Short-run shut-down point: P < AVC (TR < TVC).
steps.narration: Making a loss does not automatically mean lock the doors today. Price below average total cost misses break even. Yet staying open shrinks fixed rent losses while variable costs are covered. Only shut down immediately when price sinks below average variable cost.

steps.title: Compare demand curves, equilibrium rules, and shut-down thresholds
steps.display: Perfect competition: P = AR = MR (long run P = AC)  |  Monopoly: P = AR > MR (P > MC)  |  Shut down if P < AVC
working: Every profit-maximising firm produces where MC = MR (with MC rising).
Free entry drives long-run profit to normal in perfect competition and monopolistic competition; barriers protect monopoly.
steps.narration: Keep market structures crystal clear with one test. Every firm picks output where marginal cost meets marginal revenue. Price takers face flat demand, earning only normal profit long run. Monopolists face downward demand, charging above marginal cost. And short run survival depends on covering average variable cost.

quickCheck.stem: (Practice) In long-run equilibrium under perfect competition, which condition holds true for every firm in the industry?

options.why: When AR exceeds MR, the firm is a price maker (monopolist or monopolistic competitor), not a perfectly competitive price taker.
Correct: free entry and exit eliminate abnormal profits and losses until firms earn normal profit at minimum AC, where P = AC = AR = MC = MR.
Charging above marginal cost (P > MC) violates price-taking, and AC > AR means the firm is making a loss, which forces exit in the long run.
When price falls below average variable cost (P < AVC), the firm shuts down immediately in the short run rather than remaining in long-run equilibrium.

lessons.title: Money, inflation and the central bank

steps.title: Trading yams without swapping goats
steps.display: Barter needs a double coincidence of wants; money lets anyone trade in one step
working: Without money, you search for someone who wants your yam and sells your cloth.
With naira, trade is fast, until too much cash chases too few goods.
steps.narration: Imagine carrying yams to Balogun Market hoping a tailor wants yams for cloth. Money ends that headache instantly. It only breaks down when extra cash pushes prices up.

steps.title: Barter problems, money qualities and core functions
steps.display: Medium of exchange | Measure of value | Store of value | Standard of deferred payment
working: Barter fails from double coincidence of wants, valuation trouble, non-durability, and indivisibility.
Good money needs general acceptability, divisibility, portability, durability, homogeneity, recognisability, and controlled scarcity.
Legal tender (naira notes and kobo coins) is backed by law; cheques are representative money, not legal tender.
steps.narration: Swapping goods directly wastes hours when nobody wants what you brought. Societies invented money to fix that delay. It works because everyone accepts it, splits it easily, and carries it anywhere. Think of paying crisp naira for garri today, or promising to pay next month. Notice how cheques only represent bank cash, so sellers can refuse them.

sources.book: Comprehensive Economics by J. U. Anyaele (Oct 2003 ed.)

steps.title: Motives for holding money and money supply
steps.display: Keynes's liquidity preference: Transaction + Precautionary + Speculative motives
working: Transactions motive: cash held for daily spending like food and transport.
Precautionary motive: cash kept for emergencies such as sickness or sudden repairs.
Speculative motive: cash held to earn profit when interest rates or asset prices favour gain.
Money supply equals currency in circulation plus bank deposits, shaped by reserves and bank rate.
steps.narration: Why hold cash in your pocket instead of spending it right away? Economist John Maynard Keynes spotted three reasons. First, you buy daily bread and bus rides. Second, you save for sudden hospital bills or a flat tyre. Third, you wait to buy cheap shares or lend at higher rates. Your cash plus bank deposits form total money supply.

sources.book: Comprehensive Economics by J. U. Anyaele (Oct 2003 ed.)

steps.title: Fisher's Quantity Theory and the value of money
steps.display: MV = PT  ⇒  P = \frac{MV}{T}
working: M = money supply, V = velocity of circulation, P = general price level, T = volume of transactions.
Value of money (purchasing power) varies inversely with the general price level P.
If V and T stay constant, increasing M raises P proportionately and lowers money's purchasing power.
steps.narration: How quickly does cash jump from hand to hand? Suppose one two-naira note pays a tailor, a butcher, an electrician, and a hotelier in one day. That single note settled eight naira of business, giving a speed of four. When extra money chases unchanged goods, prices rise proportionally. Higher prices mean each naira buys fewer items.

sources.book: Comprehensive Economics by J. U. Anyaele (Oct 2003 ed.)

steps.title: Inflation, CPI measurement, types and deflation
steps.display: CPI = \frac{Current year price index}{Base year price index} × 100
working: Demand-pull inflation: excess aggregate demand over supply (e.g. deficit budgets or wage awards like Udoji 1974).
Cost-push inflation: rising production costs such as wages or imported inputs push prices up.
Inflation hurts creditors and fixed-income earners while debtors gain; hyperinflation destroys money's functions; stagflation pairs inflation with high unemployment.
Deflation is a persistent fall in prices that cuts profits and raises unemployment.
steps.narration: When prices keep climbing month after month, inflation eats your wallet. Imagine a tin of milk jumping from one hundred naira to one hundred and twenty naira. Too much buyer spending causes demand-pull inflation, while costlier fuel or wages trigger cost-push inflation. Borrowers gain because they repay with weaker cash. Falling prices, called deflation, hurt jobs instead.

sources.book: Comprehensive Economics by J. U. Anyaele (Oct 2003 ed.)

steps.title: Central Bank of Nigeria functions and monetary policy tools
steps.display: CBN (est. 1958, operational 1959): OMO, Bank Rate, Reserve Ratios, Special Deposits & Moral Suasion
working: CBN functions: sole currency issuer, federal government's banker, banker's bank, lender of last resort, and foreign reserve manager.
To curb inflation (contractionary): CBN sells securities via Open Market Operations, raises bank rate, raises cash or liquidity ratio, demands special deposits, and uses moral suasion.
Fiscal anti-inflation tools: surplus budget (cut government spending) and higher direct taxes.
To cure deflation (expansionary): CBN buys securities, lowers bank rate, and government runs a deficit budget.
steps.narration: Unlike high-street banks, the Central Bank of Nigeria never serves ordinary walk-in customers. It prints naira, holds federal funds, and rescues troubled banks as lender of last resort. Suppose inflation heats up. It sells government securities to commercial banks to drain their lending cash. Raising the discount rate and cash ratio also slows credit alongside tighter government budgets.

sources.book: Comprehensive Economics by J. U. Anyaele (Oct 2003 ed.)

steps.title: How commercial banks create credit
steps.display: Total money created = \frac{Initial deposit}{Cash reserve ratio}
working: Commercial banks keep the legal cash reserve ratio r and lend out (1 − r) of each deposit.
Loans become fresh deposits in other banks, multiplying total deposits across the banking system.
Net new credit created = Total money created − Initial deposit.
Limits: higher CBN reserve ratios, cash drain from banks, lack of collateral, and low borrowing demand.
steps.narration: How does one bank deposit multiply across the economy? Imagine you deposit ten thousand naira when the reserve rule is ten percent. Your bank keeps one thousand and lends nine thousand. That loan gets deposited elsewhere, creating another loan round. Deposits grow until total money hits one hundred thousand, though cash hoarding or scarce collateral limits it.

sources.book: Comprehensive Economics by J. U. Anyaele (Oct 2003 ed.)

steps.title: Set up Fisher's equation for the initial price level
steps.display: Problem: If M = ₦200m, V = 4, and T = 100m units, find P. If M rises to ₦300m (V, T constant), find the new P and change in money's value.
working: Formula: MV = PT  ⇒  P = \frac{MV}{T}
Initial price level: P_{1} = \frac{200 × 4}{100} = \frac{800}{100} = ₦8
steps.narration: Let us solve a quantity theory calculation step by step. Before plugging in numbers, think about what the equation tells us. Total money spent in the market equals the value of all goods traded. Here two hundred million naira changes hands four times. Dividing that total spending by one hundred million units gives eight naira per unit.

steps.title: Calculate the new price level after money supply rises
steps.display: New money supply M_{2} = ₦300m  ⇒  P_{2} = ₦12
working: Keep V = 4 and T = 100m unchanged.
steps.narration: Now the central bank lets money supply expand to three hundred million naira while speed and output stay frozen. Watch what happens to prices. Three hundred times four gives twelve hundred million naira of spending chasing the exact same one hundred million units. Dividing gives twelve naira. Notice how prices climbed cleanly whenever money grew alone.

steps.title: Compare the price rise and fall in value of money
steps.display: Price rose 50% (CPI: 150); purchasing power fell by \frac{1}{3} (33.3%)
working: Price change: \frac{12 − 8}{8} × 100 = 50%, so price index rises from 100 to 150.
Purchasing power per naira drops from \frac{1}{8} unit to \frac{1}{12} unit.
Fall in value of money: \frac{\frac{1}{8} − \frac{1}{12}}{\frac{1}{8}} × 100 = \frac{1}{3} × 100 ≈ 33.3%.
steps.narration: Pause and notice the contrast between price and purchasing power. Money supply grew by half, and the price level rose by half too, pushing our index to one hundred and fifty. Yet each naira fell from buying one eighth of a unit to one twelfth. That is a one third drop in value. Prices and value move oppositely.

steps.title: JAMB-style practice question on credit creation and CBN control
steps.display: (Practice) A bank receives a ₦50,000 deposit when the cash reserve ratio is 20%. What is the maximum total money created, and how can CBN curb resulting inflation?
working: (A) ₦100,000; by buying securities from banks
(B) ₦250,000; by selling securities to banks and raising bank rate
(C) ₦200,000; by lowering the cash reserve ratio
(D) ₦250,000; by printing more currency notes
steps.narration: Here is a practice question blending commercial bank lending with central bank tools. Notice it asks two linked things. First, how large can total deposits grow from a fifty thousand naira deposit under a twenty percent reserve rule? Second, which action cools inflation down? Let us solve the deposit total before checking the policy choices.

steps.title: Compute maximum total money created from the deposit
steps.display: Total money created = \frac{50,000}{0.20} = ₦250,000
working: Cash reserve ratio r = 20% = 0.20 = \frac{1}{5}.
Total deposits (money created) = \frac{50,000}{0.20} = 50,000 × 5 = ₦250,000.
Net new credit created = 250,000 − 50,000 = ₦200,000 (rules out ₦100,000 and ₦200,000 as total money created).
steps.narration: Divide the starting deposit by the reserve fraction, one fifth. Dividing by one fifth means multiplying by five. Five times fifty thousand gives two hundred and fifty thousand naira in total deposits. Be careful here. Two hundred thousand is only the net new credit, not the total deposits. That immediately removes two of the choices.

steps.title: Rule out wrong monetary tools to confirm the right answer
steps.display: Correct: ₦250,000; CBN sells securities to banks and raises bank rate
working: Buying securities injects cash into banks, worsening inflation.
Lowering the cash reserve ratio lets banks lend even more.
Printing extra currency increases money supply and fuels inflation.
Selling securities via OMO drains bank reserves, and raising bank rate makes borrowing costlier.
steps.narration: Now check the policy half of the remaining choices. Printing more cash obviously pushes prices even higher, not lower. Buying securities or cutting reserve rules also pumps extra credit into markets. Only selling securities to banks pulls cash out of circulation while a higher bank rate discourages borrowing. That leaves the second choice as completely accurate.

steps.title: Do not mix up commercial bank and Central Bank jobs
steps.display: Wrong: Commercial banks issue notes and set monetary policy  |  Right: Only CBN issues currency and sets policy; commercial banks take deposits and lend
working: You withdraw cash at a commercial bank counter, which tricks students into thinking it issues currency.
Only the CBN prints notes, mints coins, stabilises prices, and regulates monetary policy.
steps.narration: Students often miss easy marks here. You collect naira at a commercial bank counter, yet that bank never creates currency. Ordinary retail banks hold customer savings and give loans for profit. Meanwhile, the Central Bank alone issues legal tender. It also runs monetary policy and guards overall price stability.

sources.book: Comprehensive Economics by J. U. Anyaele (Oct 2003 ed.)

steps.title: Price level moves inversely to money value, and price controls fail under demand-pull inflation
steps.display: Wrong: Higher prices raise money's value, or price ceilings cure demand-pull inflation  |  Right: Rising prices cut purchasing power; price controls spark black markets
working: Value of money = purchasing power; when P rises, a fixed naira sum buys fewer goods.
Under demand-pull inflation, fixing maximum prices without increasing supply causes shortages, hoarding, and black markets.
steps.narration: Watch out for two related traps on inflation questions. First, higher prices never raise money's value. When food gets costlier, your naira buys less, so its value actually drops. Second, price controls rarely cure demand-pull inflation. Without extra production, buyers still chase scarce goods, creating long queues, hoarding, and thriving black markets.

sources.book: Comprehensive Economics by J. U. Anyaele (Oct 2003 ed.)

steps.title: Do not reverse Open Market Operations or confuse total deposits with net credit
steps.display: Wrong: CBN buys securities to fight inflation  |  Right: CBN sells securities to drain cash during inflation and buys during deflation
working: Inflation control: CBN sells securities to commercial banks, taking cash out of their vaults.
Deflation control: CBN buys securities from banks, injecting cash for lending.
Also check whether a question asks for total money created (\frac{D}{r}) or net new credit (\frac{D}{r} − D).
steps.narration: Exams love flipping Open Market Operations backwards. Remember whose cash changes. When the Central Bank sells securities, commercial banks pay cash to get paper, leaving less money to lend during inflation. When it buys securities, cash flows into banks to fight deflation. Also read carefully for total deposits versus net new credit.

sources.book: Comprehensive Economics by J. U. Anyaele (Oct 2003 ed.)

steps.title: Money works smoothly only when supply matches real output
steps.display: MV = PT  |  CPI tracks prices  |  CBN uses OMO, Bank Rate & Reserve Ratios
working: Money solves barter's double coincidence of wants, while CBN tools keep inflation and commercial credit in balance.
steps.narration: Keep this big picture clear for exam day. Money rescues trade from barter only when its supply stays controlled. When cash grows faster than output, prices climb and naira value falls. Always match inflation tools to draining cash, and keep commercial bank lending separate from Central Bank duties.

quickCheck.stem: (Practice) A household consumer basket costs ₦4,000 in the base year (index = 100) and rises to ₦5,000 in the current year. What is the Consumer Price Index (CPI) and the implied inflation rate?

options.why: Wrong: dividing 4,000 by 5,000 inverts the CPI formula and gives 80 instead of a rise above 100.
Correct: CPI = \frac{5,000}{4,000} × 100 = 125, so the price index rose by 125 − 100 = 25% above the base year.
Wrong: 20% uses the current price (5,000) instead of the base-year price (4,000) as the denominator.
Wrong: 125 is the price index itself; to get the percentage inflation rate you subtract the base index of 100.

lessons.title: National income and how it is measured

steps.title: One naira circling a busy street
steps.display: Your spending becomes another person's income, spinning round the economy
working: You pay a barber, the barber buys garri, and the seller pays rent.
National income adds up all that new production and earned income in one year.
steps.narration: Picture paying your barber today. That barber buys garri, and the trader pays shop rent. One naira keeps circling and creating income for everyone.

steps.title: GDP, GNP, NNP and National Income at factor cost
steps.display: GNP = GDP + NFIA;  NNP = GNP − Depreciation;  NI = NNP_{mp} − Indirect taxes + Subsidies
working: GDP = market value of final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a year.
GNP = GDP + Net Factor Income from Abroad (citizens' income abroad minus foreigners' domestic income).
NNP = GNP − Depreciation (capital consumption allowance for wear and tear of fixed capital).
National Income (NNP at factor cost) = NNP at market price − Indirect taxes + Subsidies.
steps.narration: Start with location versus citizenship. Domestic product counts everything made inside Nigeria's borders, even by foreign firms. National product tracks what Nigerian citizens earn worldwide. Suppose a Nigerian engineer earns wages in London. That counts toward our national product, not domestic product. Subtract machine wear, remove indirect taxes, and add subsidies to find factor income.

sources.book: Comprehensive Economics by J. U. Anyaele (Oct 2003 ed.)

steps.title: Per capita income and comparing living standards
steps.display: Per Capita Income = \frac{Real GNP or National Income}{Total Population}
working: Gives average income per person; total GNP can rise while per capita income falls if population grows faster.
International comparison problems: inaccurate population figures, inflation, exchange rate differences, and unequal income distribution.
Cost of living measures what a family needs for basic necessities, whereas standard of living measures real welfare.
steps.narration: Total income alone hides how crowded a country is. Dividing national income by population gives average pay per citizen. Imagine splitting ten million naira among five people. The average says two million each, even if one person keeps nine million. Faulty census counts and inflation also distort comparisons.

sources.book: Comprehensive Economics by J. U. Anyaele (Oct 2003 ed.)

steps.title: Three methods of measuring national income
steps.display: Output (Value Added) = Income = Expenditure = C + I + G + (X − M)
working: Output (product) method: sum final goods or value added (Sales − Intermediate inputs) across sectors to prevent double counting.
Income method: sum factor rewards (wages, salaries, rent, interest, profits) earned in production.
Expenditure method: sum final spending C + I + G + (X − M), where C = consumption, I = investment, G = government spending, X = exports, M = imports.
steps.narration: Economists can measure the same national pie in three ways. You can value what farms and factories produce, add up wages and profits paid out, or total what buyers spend. Think of a loaf of bread. Counting only the baker's added value above flour avoids counting wheat twice. Done carefully, all three routes match.

sources.book: Comprehensive Economics by J. U. Anyaele (Oct 2003 ed.)
Economics for Dummies by Sean Masaki Flynn

steps.title: Measurement problems, uses and limitations
steps.display: Exclude intermediate goods, transfer payments, and unrecorded non-market output
working: Problems: double counting, subsistence farming and unpaid housework, informal self-employed records, smuggling across borders, inflation, and estimating depreciation.
Uses: tracking economic growth, comparing sectors, guiding national planning, and estimating per capita income.
Limitations: ignores income inequality, non-marketed rural output, leisure, and social costs like pollution and congestion.
steps.narration: Measuring an entire country is messy in practice. Consider a village farmer eating cassava straight from her own plot. That food raises her family's welfare yet never passes through a market stall or tax ledger. Unpaid housework, smuggling, and missing shop records hide real output. High national totals also ignore pollution and unequal wealth.

sources.book: Comprehensive Economics by J. U. Anyaele (Oct 2003 ed.)
Economics for Dummies by Sean Masaki Flynn

steps.title: Circular flow of income, leakages and injections
steps.display: Leakages (Withdrawals) = S + T + M;  Injections = I + G + X
working: Two-sector model: households supply land, labour, capital, and enterprise to firms for rent, wages, interest, and profit, then spend on goods.
Three-sector model adds government: taxes (T) leak out while government spending (G) injects income; open economy adds imports (M) and exports (X).
Equilibrium occurs when total leakages equal total injections (e.g. Savings S = Investment I in a simple closed economy).
steps.narration: Income flows round between families and businesses like water in a pipe. Families sell labour to firms and spend wages back on goods. What happens when you stash part of your salary under a mattress? Savings, taxes, and imports pull money out as leakages. Meanwhile, investment, government spending, and exports push money back in.

sources.book: Comprehensive Economics by J. U. Anyaele (Oct 2003 ed.)

steps.title: Consumption, saving propensities and the multiplier
steps.display: k = \frac{1}{1 − MPC} = \frac{1}{MPS} = \frac{ΔY}{ΔI};  Y = \frac{a + I + G + (X − M)}{1 − MPC}
working: APC = \frac{C}{Y}, APS = \frac{S}{Y} (APC + APS = 1);  MPC = \frac{ΔC}{ΔY}, MPS = \frac{ΔS}{ΔY} (MPC + MPS = 1).
Autonomous consumption (a) is basic spending on food, clothing, and shelter even at zero income.
Multiplier k shows how many times an autonomous spending change ΔI multiplies into national income change ΔY = k × ΔI.
steps.narration: Your spending becomes another person's wage. One new project therefore sparks waves of fresh income. Suppose families spend eighty percent of extra pay and save twenty percent. Flipping twenty percent gives a multiplier of five. Thus, one billion naira of new investment lifts national income by five billion naira.

sources.book: Comprehensive Economics by J. U. Anyaele (Oct 2003 ed.)

steps.title: Calculate GDP at market price using the expenditure method
steps.display: Problem (₦bn): C = 500, I = 150, G = 200, X = 120, M = 90, NFIA = −30, Depreciation = 50, Indirect taxes = 60, Subsidies = 20. Find GDP, GNP, NNP and NI.
working: GDP = C + I + G + (X − M)
steps.narration: Let us walk through the full national income ladder from spending to factor earnings. Start inside the country's borders with total expenditure. Add household consumption, business investment, and government purchases together first. Then add net exports, which is exports minus imports. Putting five hundred, one hundred and fifty, two hundred, and thirty together yields eight hundred and eighty billion naira.

steps.title: Move from GDP to GNP and then subtract depreciation for NNP
steps.display: GNP = ₦850 billion;  NNP at market price = ₦800 billion
working: GNP = GDP + NFIA = 880 + (−30) = ₦850 billion
NNP = GNP − Depreciation = 850 − 50 = ₦800 billion
steps.narration: Next, shift from domestic borders to citizen ownership. Net foreign factor income is negative thirty billion here. That means foreign earners sent home more than citizens remitted back. Adding negative thirty brings gross national product to eight hundred and fifty billion. Subtracting fifty billion for worn machinery leaves eight hundred billion.

steps.title: Convert NNP at market price to National Income at factor cost
steps.display: NI (factor cost) = 800 − 60 + 20 = ₦760 billion
working: Market prices include indirect taxes (which inflate shop prices) and exclude subsidies (which lower shop prices).
NI at factor cost = NNP_{mp} − Indirect taxes + Subsidies = 800 − 60 + 20 = ₦760 billion.
steps.narration: One final adjustment gives true factor earnings. Shop prices carry indirect sales taxes that go to government, not workers or factory owners. Meanwhile, government subsidies kept shop prices artificially lower than actual production costs. So subtract sixty billion in indirect taxes and add twenty billion in subsidies. That brings national income at factor cost to seven hundred and sixty billion.

steps.title: JAMB-style practice question on equilibrium income and the multiplier
steps.display: (Practice) In a closed two-sector economy, autonomous consumption is ₦100m, investment is ₦60m, and MPC = 0.75. Find equilibrium national income Y and the change in Y if investment rises by ₦20m.
working: (A) ₦160m and ₦20m
(B) ₦640m and ₦80m
(D) ₦640m and ₦15m
steps.narration: Try this practice question on income determination and the multiplier. Notice you have two linked questions to answer. First find the resting income level when autonomous consumption is one hundred million and investment is sixty million. Then check how much an extra twenty million of investment expands income. Always compute the multiplier before touching the choices.

steps.title: Find the multiplier k and equilibrium national income Y
working: Multiplier k = \frac{1}{MPS} = \frac{1}{0.25} = 4.
Equilibrium Y = \frac{a + I}{1 − MPC} = 4 × (100 + 60) = 4 × 160 = ₦640m.
steps.narration: Subtract the consuming fraction from one to get the saving fraction, zero point two five. Dividing one by zero point two five gives a multiplier of four. Notice how dividing directly by zero point seven five would mislead you. Add one hundred and sixty million of autonomous spending. Multiplying by four yields six hundred and forty million.

steps.title: Compute the change in income and eliminate distractors
steps.display: ΔY = k × ΔI = 4 × 20 = ₦80m  ⇒  Correct: ₦640m and ₦80m
working: Rule out ₦160m and ₦20m: forgets the multiplier entirely (uses k = 1).
Rule out ₦213.3m and ₦26.7m: wrongly divides by MPC (0.75) instead of 1 − MPC (0.25).
Rule out ₦640m and ₦15m: wrongly multiplies ΔI by 0.75 instead of k = 4.
steps.narration: Now multiply that multiplier of four by the twenty million naira investment boost. Four times twenty gives eighty million naira of new national income. Look at why the other choices fail. Ignoring the multiplier leaves you at one hundred and sixty million. Multiplying twenty by zero point seven five shrinks income instead of multiplying it.

steps.title: Avoid double counting and exclude transfer payments
steps.display: Wrong: Add intermediate inputs and pensions into NI  |  Right: Count only value added (or final goods) and exclude transfer payments
working: Do not add flour's cost plus the full price of bread; count only value added at each stage.
Exclude unemployment benefits, pensions, and gifts (transfer payments) because no current good or service is produced.
steps.narration: Two items secretly inflate national income answers in exams. Never add raw materials alongside finished goods made from them. Doing so counts the exact same output twice. Also throw out transfer payments like pensions, gifts, or unemployment benefits. Recipients get cash without producing any new goods or services.

sources.book: Comprehensive Economics by J. U. Anyaele (Oct 2003 ed.)

steps.title: Do not confuse GDP with GNP or invert the multiplier
steps.display: Wrong: k = \frac{1}{MPC} or citizens abroad inside GDP  |  Right: k = \frac{1}{1 − MPC} and foreign citizen earnings sit in GNP
working: GDP depends on territory (inside Nigeria); GNP depends on nationality (citizens anywhere).
Always subtract MPC from 1 to find MPS before inverting for the multiplier k.
steps.narration: Do not mix up borders with passports. A foreign factory inside Lagos adds to Nigeria's domestic product. Meanwhile, a Nigerian doctor in London adds to our national product. Also guard the multiplier denominator carefully. Always invert the saving fraction, never the consuming fraction itself.

sources.book: Comprehensive Economics by J. U. Anyaele (Oct 2003 ed.)

steps.title: Never treat per capita income as a complete measure of welfare
steps.display: Wrong: High per capita income means everyone lives well  |  Right: Ignores distribution, subsistence output, leisure, and pollution
working: Per capita income is an average; extreme inequality can leave most citizens poor despite a high average.
GDP and NI also omit unpaid housework, rural subsistence farming, leisure hours, and environmental damage.
steps.narration: A high average income per person can easily fool you. Averages hide whether wealth sits with a tiny elite while millions struggle. Official figures also miss home-grown farm food and unpaid family care. Furthermore, extra working hours reduce leisure. Heavy factory pollution can even lift output while harming daily life.

sources.book: Comprehensive Economics by J. U. Anyaele (Oct 2003 ed.)
Economics for Dummies by Sean Masaki Flynn

steps.title: Measure every naira once and track how spending multiplies
steps.display: GDP + NFIA = GNP  |  GNP − Dep = NNP  |  Output = Income = Expenditure  |  k = \frac{1}{MPS}
working: Exclude intermediate inputs and transfer payments, then apply k = \frac{1}{1 − MPC} to track autonomous spending shifts.
steps.narration: Remember these four pillars for national income questions. Count output, income, or spending once by dropping intermediate inputs and transfer payments. Step cleanly from domestic output to national product and net factor cost. Finally, invert the saving propensity. That tells you how strongly new spending multiplies through the circular flow.

quickCheck.stem: (Practice) In calculating national income by the income method, a country records wages of ₦400m, rent of ₦80m, interest of ₦50m, profits of ₦120m, and unemployment benefits of ₦45m. What is the domestic factor income?

options.why: Correct: domestic factor income sums wages, rent, interest, and profits (400 + 80 + 50 + 120 = ₦650m) and excludes unemployment benefits as transfer payments.
Wrong: ₦695m mistakenly includes ₦45m of unemployment benefits, which are transfer payments not earned from current production.
Wrong: ₦530m leaves out business profits (₦120m), which are the factor reward for enterprise.
Wrong: ₦605m subtracts the ₦45m transfer payment from ₦650m instead of simply ignoring transfer payments.
